questions.question_text: Let C be a circle having centre in the first quadrant and touching the $x$ -axis at a distance of 3 units from the origin. If the circle $C$ has an intercept of length $6\sqrt{3}$ on $y$ -axis, then the length of the chord of the circle C on the line $x-y=3$ is :
questions.question_html: Let C be a circle having centre in the first quadrant and touching the $x$ -axis at a distance of 3 units from the origin. If the circle $C$ has an intercept of length $6\sqrt{3}$ on $y$ -axis, then the length of the chord of the circle C on the line $x-y=3$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Since the circle touches the $x$ -axis at a point which is $3$ units from the origin, the point of contact is $(3,0)$ . The centre lies in the first quadrant and the radius is perpendicular to the tangent at the point of contact. So, the centre must be of the form $(3,r)$ , where $r$ is the radius. The circle has an intercept of length $6\sqrt{3}$ on the $y$ -axis. This means the chord cut by the line $x=0$ has length $6\sqrt{3}$ . For a circle of radius $r$ , if the distance of a chord from the centre is $d$ , then chord length is $2\sqrt{r^{2}-d^{2}}$ . Here, the distance from centre $(3,r)$ to the $y$ -axis $(x=0)$ is $d=3$ . So the intercept on the $y$ -axis is $2\sqrt{r^{2}-3^{2}}=6\sqrt{3}$ So, $\sqrt{r^{2}-9}=3\sqrt{3} \Rightarrow r^{2}-9=27 \Rightarrow r^{2}=36 \Rightarrow r=6$ Hence, centre of the circle is $(3,6)$ and radius is $6$ units. Now we need the length of the chord cut by the line $x-y=3$ . First find the perpendicular distance $p$ from the centre $(3,6)$ to the line $x-y-3=0$ : $p=\frac{|1 \cdot 3+(-1) \cdot 6-3|}{\sqrt{1^{2}+(-1)^{2}}}=\frac{|3-6-3|}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}}$ Now chord length on this line is $PQ=2\sqrt{6^{2}-p^{2}} \therefore p=\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\begin{aligned} & p=\frac{|3-6-3|}{\sqrt{2}} \\ & PQ=2\sqrt{36-\frac{36}{2}} \\ & =2 \times \frac{6}{\sqrt{2}}=6\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Since the circle touches the $x$ -axis at a point which is $3$ units from the origin, the point of contact is $(3,0)$ .

The centre lies in the first quadrant and the radius is perpendicular to the tangent at the point of contact. So, the centre must be of the form $(3,r)$ , where $r$ is the radius.

The circle has an intercept of length $6\sqrt{3}$ on the $y$ -axis. This means the chord cut by the line $x=0$ has length $6\sqrt{3}$ .

For a circle of radius $r$ , if the distance of a chord from the centre is $d$ , then chord length is $2\sqrt{r^{2}-d^{2}}$ .

Here, the distance from centre $(3,r)$ to the $y$ -axis $(x=0)$ is $d=3$ . So the intercept on the $y$ -axis is

$2\sqrt{r^{2}-3^{2}}=6\sqrt{3}$

So,

$\sqrt{r^{2}-9}=3\sqrt{3} \Rightarrow r^{2}-9=27 \Rightarrow r^{2}=36 \Rightarrow r=6$

Hence, centre of the circle is $(3,6)$ and radius is $6$ units.

Now we need the length of the chord cut by the line $x-y=3$ .

First find the perpendicular distance $p$ from the centre $(3,6)$ to the line $x-y-3=0$ :

$p=\frac{|1 \cdot 3+(-1) \cdot 6-3|}{\sqrt{1^{2}+(-1)^{2}}}=\frac{|3-6-3|}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}}$

Now chord length on this line is

$PQ=2\sqrt{6^{2}-p^{2}} \therefore p=\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}}$

$\begin{aligned} & p=\frac{|3-6-3|}{\sqrt{2}} \\ & PQ=2\sqrt{36-\frac{36}{2}} \\ & =2 \times \frac{6}{\sqrt{2}}=6\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let a circle pass through the origin and its centre be the point of intersection of two mutually perpendicular lines $x+(k-1)y+3=0$ and $2x+k^{2}y-4=0$ . If the line $x-y+2=0$ intersects the circle at the points A and B, then $(AB)^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let a circle pass through the origin and its centre be the point of intersection of two mutually perpendicular lines $x+(k-1)y+3=0$ and $2x+k^{2}y-4=0$ . If the line $x-y+2=0$ intersects the circle at the points A and B, then $(AB)^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & x+(k-1)y+3=0 \\ & 2x+k^{2}y-4=0 \\ & (\frac{1}{1-k})(\frac{2}{k^{2}})=1 \\ & 2=k^{2}-k^{3} \\ & k^{3}-k^{2}+2=0 \\ & k=-1 \end{aligned}$ Solving : $\begin{aligned} & 2(x-2y+3)=0 \\ & 2x+y-4=0 \\ & -5y+10=0 \\ & y=2 \end{aligned}$ $x=1$ Centre $(1,2)$ $r=\sqrt{5}$ So circle is $(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=5$ Chord $x-y+2=0$ $\begin{aligned} & p=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ & \ell=\sqrt{5-\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \\ & AB=\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}} \therefore AB^{2}=18 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & x+(k-1)y+3=0 \\ & 2x+k^{2}y-4=0 \\ & (\frac{1}{1-k})(\frac{2}{k^{2}})=1 \\ & 2=k^{2}-k^{3} \\ & k^{3}-k^{2}+2=0 \\ & k=-1 \end{aligned}$

Solving :

$\begin{aligned} & 2(x-2y+3)=0 \\ & 2x+y-4=0 \\ & -5y+10=0 \\ & y=2 \end{aligned}$

$x=1$

Centre $(1,2)$

$r=\sqrt{5}$

So circle is $(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=5$

Chord $x-y+2=0$

$\begin{aligned} & p=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ & \ell=\sqrt{5-\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \\ & AB=\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}} \therefore AB^{2}=18 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let a circle C have its centre in the first quadrant, intersect the coordinate axes at exactly three points and cut off equal intercepts from the coordinate axes. If the length of the chord of C on the line $x+y=1$ is $\sqrt{14}$ , then the square of the radius of C is ________.
questions.question_html: Let a circle C have its centre in the first quadrant, intersect the coordinate axes at exactly three points and cut off equal intercepts from the coordinate axes. If the length of the chord of C on the line $x+y=1$ is $\sqrt{14}$ , then the square of the radius of C is ________.
questions.explanation_html: $\begin{aligned} & r^{2}=(\frac{\sqrt{14}}{2})^{2}+(r-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})^{2} \\ & r^{2}=\frac{7}{2}+r^{2}-\sqrt{2}r+\frac{1}{2} \\ & \sqrt{2}r=4 \\ & r=2\sqrt{2} \\ & r^{2}=8 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let the point P be the vertex of the parabola $y=x^{2}-6x+12$ . If a line passing through the point P intersects the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-2x-4y+3=0$ at the points R and S , then the maximum value of $(PR+PS)^{2}$ is :
questions.question_html: Let the point P be the vertex of the parabola $y=x^{2}-6x+12$ . If a line passing through the point P intersects the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-2x-4y+3=0$ at the points R and S , then the maximum value of $(PR+PS)^{2}$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Vertex of the parabola $y=x^{2}-6x+12$ is found by completing the square: $y=(x-3)^{2}+3$ So, the vertex is $P=(3,3)$ Now the circle is $x^{2}+y^{2}-2x-4y+3=0$ Complete squares: $(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=2$ Hence, the centre of the circle is $C=(1,2)$ and radius is $r=\sqrt{2}$ Now, $PC=\sqrt{(3-1)^{2}+(3-2)^{2}}=\sqrt{4+1}=\sqrt{5}$ Since the line through $P$ cuts the circle at $R$ and $S$ , the line must intersect the circle in a chord $RS$ . Let the perpendicular distance from the centre $C$ to this line be $d$ . Then chord length $RS=2\sqrt{r^{2}-d^{2}}=2\sqrt{2-d^{2}}$ Also, since $P$ lies on the line outside the circle, and $R,S$ are the intersection points on opposite sides along the line, we have $PR+PS=RS$ only if $P$ lies between them, which is not possible here because $P$ is outside the circle. So let us use power of a point. If $PR$ and $PS$ are the two secant segments from $P$ , then $PR \cdot PS=PC^{2}-r^{2}=5-2=3$ Let the line make an angle such that the foot from $C$ to the line gives distance $d$ . If $M$ is the midpoint of chord $RS$ , then $CM=d,PM=\sqrt{PC^{2}-d^{2}}=\sqrt{5-d^{2}}$ because in right triangle with hypotenuse $PC$ . Also $MR=MS=\sqrt{r^{2}-d^{2}}=\sqrt{2-d^{2}}$ Since $P$ is outside the circle, along the secant line, $PR=PM-MR,PS=PM+MR$ Therefore, $PR+PS=2PM=2\sqrt{5-d^{2}}$ So $(PR+PS)^{2}=4(5-d^{2})$ To maximize this, we must minimize $d^{2}$ . The minimum possible value of $d$ is $0$ , when the line passes through the centre $C$ . Hence maximum value is $(PR+PS)_{max}^{2}=4 \times 5=20$ Therefore, the required maximum value is $20$ So the correct option is B .
questions.explanation_html:
Vertex of the parabola

$y=x^{2}-6x+12$

is found by completing the square:

$y=(x-3)^{2}+3$

So, the vertex is

$P=(3,3)$

Now the circle is

$x^{2}+y^{2}-2x-4y+3=0$

Complete squares:

$(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=2$

Hence, the centre of the circle is

$C=(1,2)$

and radius is

$r=\sqrt{2}$

Now,

$PC=\sqrt{(3-1)^{2}+(3-2)^{2}}=\sqrt{4+1}=\sqrt{5}$

Since the line through $P$ cuts the circle at $R$ and $S$ , the line must intersect the circle in a chord $RS$ .

Let the perpendicular distance from the centre $C$ to this line be $d$ .

Then chord length

$RS=2\sqrt{r^{2}-d^{2}}=2\sqrt{2-d^{2}}$

Also, since $P$ lies on the line outside the circle, and $R,S$ are the intersection points on opposite sides along the line, we have

$PR+PS=RS$

only if $P$ lies between them, which is not possible here because $P$ is outside the circle.

So let us use power of a point.

If $PR$ and $PS$ are the two secant segments from $P$ , then

$PR \cdot PS=PC^{2}-r^{2}=5-2=3$

Let the line make an angle such that the foot from $C$ to the line gives distance $d$ .

If $M$ is the midpoint of chord $RS$ , then

$CM=d,PM=\sqrt{PC^{2}-d^{2}}=\sqrt{5-d^{2}}$

because in right triangle with hypotenuse $PC$ .

Also

$MR=MS=\sqrt{r^{2}-d^{2}}=\sqrt{2-d^{2}}$

Since $P$ is outside the circle, along the secant line,

$PR=PM-MR,PS=PM+MR$

Therefore,

$PR+PS=2PM=2\sqrt{5-d^{2}}$

So

$(PR+PS)^{2}=4(5-d^{2})$

To maximize this, we must minimize $d^{2}$ .

The minimum possible value of $d$ is $0$ , when the line passes through the centre $C$ .

Hence maximum value is

$(PR+PS)_{max}^{2}=4 \times 5=20$

Therefore, the required maximum value is

$20$

So the correct option is B.

questions.question_text: Let the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=4$ intersect x-axis at the points A $(a,0)$ , $a>0$ and B $(b,0)$ . Let $P(2cos\alpha,2sin\alpha)$ , $0<\alpha<\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $Q(2cos\beta,2sin\beta)$ be two points such that $(\alpha-\beta)=\frac{\pi}{2}$ . Then the point of intersection of AQ and BP lies on :
questions.question_html: Let the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=4$ intersect x-axis at the points A $(a,0)$ , $a>0$ and B $(b,0)$ . Let $P(2cos\alpha,2sin\alpha)$ , $0<\alpha<\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $Q(2cos\beta,2sin\beta)$ be two points such that $(\alpha-\beta)=\frac{\pi}{2}$ . Then the point of intersection of AQ and BP lies on :
questions.explanation_text: The circle is $x^{2}+y^{2}=2^{2}$ (radius $r=2$ ). Intersection with $x$ -axis: Setting $y=0$ gives $x^{2}=4 \Rightarrow x= \pm 2$ . Since $a>0,A=(2,0)$ . Therefore, $B=(-2,0)$ . Points $P$ and $Q$ : $P=(2cos\alpha,2sin\alpha)$ $Q=(2cos\beta,2sin\beta)$ Let point of intersection of $AQ$ .& $BP$ be $R(ℎ,k)$ . So, we need to find locus of points of intersection of $AQ&BP$ . Slope of $BP=$ slope of $BR$ $\begin{aligned} \frac{k-0}{ℎ-(-2)}=\frac{2sin\alpha-0}{2cos\alpha+2} \\ \frac{k}{ℎ+2}=\frac{sin\alpha}{cos\alpha+1} \Rightarrow \frac{k}{ℎ+2}=\frac{2sin\frac{\alpha}{2}cos\frac{\alpha}{2}}{2cos^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}} \\ \frac{k}{ℎ+2}=tan\frac{\alpha}{2}...(i) \end{aligned}$ Similarly, slope of $QA=$ slope of $QR$ $\begin{aligned} \frac{2sin\beta-0}{2cos\beta-2}=\frac{k-0}{ℎ-2} \\ \frac{sin\beta}{cos\beta-1}=\frac{k}{ℎ-2} \Rightarrow \frac{2sin\frac{\beta}{2}cos\frac{\beta}{2}}{-2sin^{2}\frac{\beta}{2}}=\frac{k}{ℎ-2} \\ -cot\frac{\beta}{2}=\frac{k}{ℎ-2} \\ cot\frac{\beta}{2}=\frac{k}{2-ℎ} \Rightarrow tan\frac{\beta}{2}=\frac{2-ℎ}{k} \end{aligned}$ Given, $\begin{aligned} \alpha-\beta=\frac{\pi}{2} \Rightarrow \frac{\alpha}{2}-\frac{\beta}{2}=\frac{\pi}{4} \\ tan(\frac{\alpha}{2}-\frac{\beta}{2})=tan\frac{\pi}{4} \\ \frac{tan\frac{\alpha}{2}-tan\frac{\beta}{2}}{1+tan\frac{\alpha}{2}tan\frac{\beta}{2}}=1 \end{aligned}$ Substitute $tan\frac{\alpha}{2}=\frac{k}{ℎ+2},tan\frac{\beta}{2}=\frac{2-ℎ}{k}$ $\begin{aligned} \frac{\frac{k}{ℎ+2}-\frac{2-ℎ}{k}}{1+(\frac{k}{ℎ+2})(\frac{2-ℎ}{k})}=1 \\ \frac{k}{ℎ+2}+\frac{ℎ-2}{k}=1+(\frac{k}{ℎ+2})(\frac{2-ℎ}{k}) \\ \frac{k^{2}+ℎ^{2}-4}{(ℎ+2)k}=\frac{4k}{(ℎ+2)k} \\ \frac{k^{2}+ℎ^{2}-4}{(ℎ+2)k}=\frac{4k}{(ℎ+2)k} \\ k^{2}+ℎ^{2}-4=4k \\ k^{2}+ℎ^{2}-4k-4=0 \end{aligned}$ Replace $(ℎ,k) \rightarrow (x,y)$ $x^{2}+y^{2}-4y-4=0$
questions.explanation_html:
The circle is $x^{2}+y^{2}=2^{2}$ (radius $r=2$ ).

  • Intersection with $x$ -axis: Setting $y=0$ gives $x^{2}=4 \Rightarrow x= \pm 2$ .

  • Since $a>0,A=(2,0)$ .

  • Therefore, $B=(-2,0)$ .

  • Points $P$ and $Q$ :

  • $P=(2cos\alpha,2sin\alpha)$

  • $Q=(2cos\beta,2sin\beta)$

Let point of intersection of $AQ$ .& $BP$ be $R(ℎ,k)$ .

So, we need to find locus of points of intersection of $AQ&BP$ .

Slope of $BP=$ slope of $BR$

$\begin{aligned} \frac{k-0}{ℎ-(-2)}=\frac{2sin\alpha-0}{2cos\alpha+2} \\ \frac{k}{ℎ+2}=\frac{sin\alpha}{cos\alpha+1} \Rightarrow \frac{k}{ℎ+2}=\frac{2sin\frac{\alpha}{2}cos\frac{\alpha}{2}}{2cos^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}} \\ \frac{k}{ℎ+2}=tan\frac{\alpha}{2}...(i) \end{aligned}$

Similarly, slope of $QA=$ slope of $QR$

$\begin{aligned} \frac{2sin\beta-0}{2cos\beta-2}=\frac{k-0}{ℎ-2} \\ \frac{sin\beta}{cos\beta-1}=\frac{k}{ℎ-2} \Rightarrow \frac{2sin\frac{\beta}{2}cos\frac{\beta}{2}}{-2sin^{2}\frac{\beta}{2}}=\frac{k}{ℎ-2} \\ -cot\frac{\beta}{2}=\frac{k}{ℎ-2} \\ cot\frac{\beta}{2}=\frac{k}{2-ℎ} \Rightarrow tan\frac{\beta}{2}=\frac{2-ℎ}{k} \end{aligned}$

Given,

$\begin{aligned} \alpha-\beta=\frac{\pi}{2} \Rightarrow \frac{\alpha}{2}-\frac{\beta}{2}=\frac{\pi}{4} \\ tan(\frac{\alpha}{2}-\frac{\beta}{2})=tan\frac{\pi}{4} \\ \frac{tan\frac{\alpha}{2}-tan\frac{\beta}{2}}{1+tan\frac{\alpha}{2}tan\frac{\beta}{2}}=1 \end{aligned}$

Substitute

$tan\frac{\alpha}{2}=\frac{k}{ℎ+2},tan\frac{\beta}{2}=\frac{2-ℎ}{k}$

$\begin{aligned} \frac{\frac{k}{ℎ+2}-\frac{2-ℎ}{k}}{1+(\frac{k}{ℎ+2})(\frac{2-ℎ}{k})}=1 \\ \frac{k}{ℎ+2}+\frac{ℎ-2}{k}=1+(\frac{k}{ℎ+2})(\frac{2-ℎ}{k}) \\ \frac{k^{2}+ℎ^{2}-4}{(ℎ+2)k}=\frac{4k}{(ℎ+2)k} \\ \frac{k^{2}+ℎ^{2}-4}{(ℎ+2)k}=\frac{4k}{(ℎ+2)k} \\ k^{2}+ℎ^{2}-4=4k \\ k^{2}+ℎ^{2}-4k-4=0 \end{aligned}$

Replace $(ℎ,k) \rightarrow (x,y)$

$x^{2}+y^{2}-4y-4=0$

questions.question_text: If $P$ is a point on the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=4,Q$ is a point on the straight line $5x+y+2=0$ and $x-y+1=0$ is the perpendicular bisector of PQ , then 13 times the sum of abscissa of all such points P is $____$ .
questions.question_html: If $P$ is a point on the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=4,Q$ is a point on the straight line $5x+y+2=0$ and $x-y+1=0$ is the perpendicular bisector of PQ , then 13 times the sum of abscissa of all such points P is $____$ .
questions.explanation_text: $P(x_{1}y_{1})$ and point $Q(x_{2},y_{2})$ Mid point of $PQM=(\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}}{2},\frac{y_{1}+y_{2}}{2})$ Substitute M into $x-y+1=0$ $x_{1}+x_{2}-y_{1}-y_{2}+2=0..(i)$ Slope of PQ is Perpendicular to slope of bisector line So, slope of $PQ=-1$ $y_{2}=x_{1}-x_{2}+y_{1}\dots..(ii)$ $Q(x_{2},y_{2})$ lie on $5x+y+2=0$ So, $5x_{2}+y_{2}+2=0\dots\dots$ . (iii) Substitute (iii) in (i) $x_{2}=\frac{-x_{1}-y_{1}-2}{4}\dots.(iv)$ Substitute (iii) in (ii) $x_{2}=y_{1}-1\dots..(v)$ From (iv) and (v) $x_{1}=2-5y$ $(x_{1},y_{1})$ lie on circle $x_{1}^{2}+y_{1}^{2}=4$ Pt $x_{1}=2-5y_{1}$ $y_{1}=0,-\frac{10}{13}$ So, $x_{1}=2,\frac{-24}{13}$ So, $2+(-\frac{24}{13})=\frac{2}{13}$ So, $13 \times \frac{2}{13}=2$
questions.explanation_html:
$P(x_{1}y_{1})$ and point $Q(x_{2},y_{2})$

Mid point of $PQM=(\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}}{2},\frac{y_{1}+y_{2}}{2})$

Substitute M into $x-y+1=0$

$x_{1}+x_{2}-y_{1}-y_{2}+2=0..(i)$

Slope of PQ is Perpendicular to slope of bisector line So, slope of $PQ=-1$

$y_{2}=x_{1}-x_{2}+y_{1}\dots..(ii)$

$Q(x_{2},y_{2})$ lie on $5x+y+2=0$

So, $5x_{2}+y_{2}+2=0\dots\dots$ . (iii)

Substitute (iii) in (i)

$x_{2}=\frac{-x_{1}-y_{1}-2}{4}\dots.(iv)$

Substitute (iii) in (ii)

$x_{2}=y_{1}-1\dots..(v)$

From (iv) and (v)

$x_{1}=2-5y$

$(x_{1},y_{1})$ lie on circle

$x_{1}^{2}+y_{1}^{2}=4$

Pt $x_{1}=2-5y_{1}$

$y_{1}=0,-\frac{10}{13}$

So, $x_{1}=2,\frac{-24}{13}$

So, $2+(-\frac{24}{13})=\frac{2}{13}$

So, $13 \times \frac{2}{13}=2$

questions.question_text: Let P be a moving point on the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-6x-8y+21=0$ . Then, the maximum distance of P from the vertex of the parabola $x^{2}+6x+y+13=0$ is equal to:
questions.question_html: Let P be a moving point on the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-6x-8y+21=0$ . Then, the maximum distance of P from the vertex of the parabola $x^{2}+6x+y+13=0$ is equal to:
questions.explanation_text: First, find the vertex of the parabola. The parabola is $x^{2}+6x+y+13=0$ Rewrite it by completing the square: $x^{2}+6x+y+13=0$ $x^{2}+6x+9+y+13-9=0$ $(x+3)^{2}+y+4=0$ $y=-(x+3)^{2}-4$ So, the vertex of the parabola is $(-3,-4)$ Now, find the centre and radius of the circle. Given circle: $x^{2}+y^{2}-6x-8y+21=0$ Complete the squares: $x^{2}-6x+y^{2}-8y+21=0$ $(x^{2}-6x+9)+(y^{2}-8y+16)+21-9-16=0$ $(x-3)^{2}+(y-4)^{2}-4=0$ $(x-3)^{2}+(y-4)^{2}=4$ Hence, centre of the circle is $(3,4)$ and radius is $r=2$ Now we need the maximum distance of a point $P$ on this circle from the vertex $(-3,-4)$ . Let $V=(-3,-4)$ and centre of circle be $C=(3,4)$ . First find $VC$ : $VC=\sqrt{(3+3)^{2}+(4+4)^{2}}=\sqrt{6^{2}+8^{2}}=\sqrt{36+64}=\sqrt{100}=10$ For a point moving on a circle, the maximum distance from an external point is $VC+r$ So, $\text{Maximum distance}=10+2=12$ Therefore, the correct answer is $12$ So, Option C is correct.

questions.question_text: Let $y=x$ be the equation of a chord of the circle $C_{1}$ (in the closed half-plane $x \ge 0$ ) of diameter 10 passing through the origin. Let $C_{2}$ be another circle described on the given chord as its diameter. If the equation of the chord of the circle $C_{2}$ , which passes through the point $(2,3)$ and is farthest from the center of $C_{2}$ , is $x+ay+b=0$ , then $a-b$ is equal to
questions.question_html: Let $y=x$ be the equation of a chord of the circle $C_{1}$ (in the closed half-plane $x \ge 0$ ) of diameter 10 passing through the origin. Let $C_{2}$ be another circle described on the given chord as its diameter. If the equation of the chord of the circle $C_{2}$ , which passes through the point $(2,3)$ and is farthest from the center of $C_{2}$ , is $x+ay+b=0$ , then $a-b$ is equal to
questions.explanation_text: To find the value of $a-b$ , Determine the equation of circle $C_{1}$ The circle $C_{1}$ has a diameter of 10 , so its radius is $R=5$ . It passes through the origin ( 0,0 ) and is contained in the closed half-plane $x \ge 0$ . Let the center of $C_{1}$ be $(ℎ,k)$ . Since it passes through $(0,0)$ , we have $ℎ^{2}+k^{2}=R^{2}=25$ . For the circle to lie entirely in the region $x \ge 0$ while passing through $(0,0)$ , the distance from the center to the $y$ -axis must be equal to the radius, and the center must have a non-negative $x$ -coordinate. Thus, $ℎ=R=5$ . Substituting $ℎ=5$ into $ℎ^{2}+k^{2}=25$ gives $25+k^{2}=25$ , which implies $k=0$ . The equation of $C_{1}$ is: $(x-5)^{2}+y^{2}=25$ Find the center of circle $C_{2}$ The line $y=x$ is a chord of $C_{1}$ . We find the intersection points of $y=x$ and $C_{1}$ : $(x-5)^{2}+x^{2}=25$ $\Rightarrow$ $x^{2}-10x+25+x^{2}=25$ $\Rightarrow$ $2x^{2}-10x=0$ $\Rightarrow$ $2x(x-5)=0$ The intersection points are $(0,0)$ and $(5,5)$ . These are the endpoints of the diameter of circle $C_{2}$ . The center $M$ of $C_{2}$ is the midpoint of the chord: $M=(\frac{0+5}{2},\frac{0+5}{2})=(2.5,2.5)$ Determine the equation of the chord of $C_{2}$ We are looking for the equation of a chord of $C_{2}$ passing through $P(2,3)$ that is farthest from the center $M(2.5,2.5)$ . In any circle, the chord passing through a point $P$ that is farthest from the center is the one perpendicular to the radius (or segment) $MP$ . The slope of the segment $MP$ is: $m_{MP}=\frac{3-2.5}{2-2.5}=\frac{0.5}{-0.5}=-1$ The slope $m$ of the required chord is the negative reciprocal of $m_{MP}$ : $m=-\frac{1}{-1}=1$ Using the point-slope form for the line through $P(2,3)$ with slope $m=1$ : $y-3=1(x-2)$ $\Rightarrow$ $y-3=x-2$ $\Rightarrow$ $x-y+1=0$ Calculate $a-b$ The equation is given in the form $x+ay+b=0$ . Comparing this to $x-y+1=0$ , we identify: $\begin{aligned} & a=-1 \\ & b=1 \end{aligned}$ Finally, we calculate the required value: $a-b=-1-1=-2$
questions.explanation_html:
To find the value of $a-b$ ,

Determine the equation of circle $C_{1}$

The circle $C_{1}$ has a diameter of 10 , so its radius is $R=5$ . It passes through the origin ( 0,0 ) and is contained in the closed half-plane $x \ge 0$ .

Let the center of $C_{1}$ be $(ℎ,k)$ . Since it passes through $(0,0)$ , we have $ℎ^{2}+k^{2}=R^{2}=25$ .

For the circle to lie entirely in the region $x \ge 0$ while passing through $(0,0)$ , the distance from the center to the $y$ -axis must be equal to the radius, and the center must have a non-negative $x$ -coordinate.

Thus, $ℎ=R=5$ .

Substituting $ℎ=5$ into $ℎ^{2}+k^{2}=25$ gives $25+k^{2}=25$ , which implies $k=0$ .

The equation of $C_{1}$ is:

$(x-5)^{2}+y^{2}=25$

Find the center of circle $C_{2}$

The line $y=x$ is a chord of $C_{1}$ . We find the intersection points of $y=x$ and $C_{1}$ :

$(x-5)^{2}+x^{2}=25$

$\Rightarrow$ $x^{2}-10x+25+x^{2}=25$

$\Rightarrow$ $2x^{2}-10x=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $2x(x-5)=0$

The intersection points are $(0,0)$ and $(5,5)$ . These are the endpoints of the diameter of circle $C_{2}$ .

The center $M$ of $C_{2}$ is the midpoint of the chord:

$M=(\frac{0+5}{2},\frac{0+5}{2})=(2.5,2.5)$

Determine the equation of the chord of $C_{2}$

We are looking for the equation of a chord of $C_{2}$ passing through $P(2,3)$ that is farthest from the center $M(2.5,2.5)$ .

In any circle, the chord passing through a point $P$ that is farthest from the center is the one perpendicular to the radius (or segment) $MP$ .

The slope of the segment $MP$ is:

$m_{MP}=\frac{3-2.5}{2-2.5}=\frac{0.5}{-0.5}=-1$

The slope $m$ of the required chord is the negative reciprocal of $m_{MP}$ :

$m=-\frac{1}{-1}=1$

Using the point-slope form for the line through $P(2,3)$ with slope $m=1$ :

$y-3=1(x-2)$

$\Rightarrow$ $y-3=x-2$ $\Rightarrow$ $x-y+1=0$

Calculate $a-b$

The equation is given in the form $x+ay+b=0$ . Comparing this to $x-y+1=0$ , we identify:

$\begin{aligned} & a=-1 \\ & b=1 \end{aligned}$

Finally, we calculate the required value:

$a-b=-1-1=-2$

questions.question_html: Suppose that two chords, drawn from the point $(1,2)$ on the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}+x-3y=0$ are bisected by the $y$ -axis. If the other ends of these chords are R and S , and the mid point of the line segment RS is $(\alpha,\beta)$ , then $6(\alpha+\beta)$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: The given circle is $x^{2}+y^{2}+x-3y=0$ and the point from which the two chords are drawn is $P(1,2)$ We are told that these chords are bisected by the $y$ -axis. Let the other end of one such chord be $R(x,y)$ . Since the chord joining $P(1,2)$ and $R(x,y)$ is bisected by the $y$ -axis, its midpoint must lie on the $y$ -axis. So the $x$ -coordinate of the midpoint is $0$ . Midpoint of $P(1,2)$ and $R(x,y)$ is $(\frac{1+x}{2},\frac{2+y}{2})$ Since this lies on the $y$ -axis, $\frac{1+x}{2}=0$ So, $x=-1$ Thus, the other end of each such chord must lie on the line $x=-1$ Now find where this line cuts the circle. Substitute $x=-1$ in $x^{2}+y^{2}+x-3y=0$ We get $(-1)^{2}+y^{2}+(-1)-3y=0$ $1+y^{2}-1-3y=0$ $y^{2}-3y=0$ $y(y-3)=0$ So, $y=0\text{or}y=3$ Hence the two points are $R(-1,0),S(-1,3)$ Now midpoint of $RS$ is $(\alpha,\beta)=(\frac{-1+(-1)}{2},\frac{0+3}{2})$ $(\alpha,\beta)=(-1,\frac{3}{2})$ Therefore, $\alpha+\beta=-1+\frac{3}{2}=\frac{1}{2}$ So, $6(\alpha+\beta)=6 \cdot \frac{1}{2}=3$ Hence the correct answer is $3$ So, the correct option is Option B .
questions.explanation_html:
The given circle is

$x^{2}+y^{2}+x-3y=0$

and the point from which the two chords are drawn is

$P(1,2)$

We are told that these chords are bisected by the $y$ -axis.

Let the other end of one such chord be $R(x,y)$ .

Since the chord joining $P(1,2)$ and $R(x,y)$ is bisected by the $y$ -axis, its midpoint must lie on the $y$ -axis.

So the $x$ -coordinate of the midpoint is $0$ .

Midpoint of $P(1,2)$ and $R(x,y)$ is

$(\frac{1+x}{2},\frac{2+y}{2})$

Since this lies on the $y$ -axis,

$\frac{1+x}{2}=0$

So,

$x=-1$

Thus, the other end of each such chord must lie on the line

$x=-1$

Now find where this line cuts the circle.

Substitute $x=-1$ in

$x^{2}+y^{2}+x-3y=0$

We get

$(-1)^{2}+y^{2}+(-1)-3y=0$

$1+y^{2}-1-3y=0$

$y^{2}-3y=0$

$y(y-3)=0$

So,

$y=0\text{or}y=3$

Hence the two points are

$R(-1,0),S(-1,3)$

Now midpoint of $RS$ is

$(\alpha,\beta)=(\frac{-1+(-1)}{2},\frac{0+3}{2})$

$(\alpha,\beta)=(-1,\frac{3}{2})$

Therefore,

$\alpha+\beta=-1+\frac{3}{2}=\frac{1}{2}$

So,

$6(\alpha+\beta)=6 \cdot \frac{1}{2}=3$

Hence the correct answer is

$3$

So, the correct option is Option B.

questions.question_text: Let $C$ be the circle $x^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=2,E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ be two ellipses whose centres lie at the origin and major axes lie on x -axis and y -axis respectively. Let the straight line $x+y=3$ touch the curves $C,E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ at $P(x_{1},y_{1}),Q(x_{2},y_{2})$ and $R(x_{3},y_{3})$ respectively. Given that $P$ is the mid point of the line segment $QR$ and $PQ=\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}$ , the value of $9(x_{1}y_{1}+x_{2}y_{2}+x_{3}y_{3})$ is equal to _______.
questions.question_html: Let $C$ be the circle $x^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=2,E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ be two ellipses whose centres lie at the origin and major axes lie on x -axis and y -axis respectively. Let the straight line $x+y=3$ touch the curves $C,E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ at $P(x_{1},y_{1}),Q(x_{2},y_{2})$ and $R(x_{3},y_{3})$ respectively. Given that $P$ is the mid point of the line segment $QR$ and $PQ=\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}$ , the value of $9(x_{1}y_{1}+x_{2}y_{2}+x_{3}y_{3})$ is equal to _______.
questions.explanation_text: Solving the line $x+y=3$ , and the circle $x^{2}+$ $(y-1)^{2}=2$ Substitute $y=3-x$ : $\begin{aligned} & x^{2}+(3-x-1)^{2}=2 \\ & \Rightarrow x^{2}-2x+1=0 \\ & \Rightarrow x=1 \Rightarrow y=2 \end{aligned}$ So, $P=(x_{1},y_{1})=(1,2) \Rightarrow x_{1}y_{1}=1 \cdot 2=2$ Use midpoint condition Let $Q=(x_{2},y_{2}),R=(x_{3},y_{3})$ . Since $P$ is the midpoint of QR: $$x_2+x_3=2 x_1=2, y_2+y_3=2 y_1=4 $$So, we can write: $x_{3}=2-x_{2},y_{3}=4-y_{2}$ Given, $PQ=\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} \Rightarrow PQ^{2}=(x_{2}-1)^{2}+(y_{2}-2)^{2}=\frac{8}{9}$ Let's denote: $x_{2}=a,y_{2}=b,x_{3}=2-a,y_{3}=4-b$ $\begin{aligned} & (a-1)^{2}+(b-2)^{2}=\frac{8}{9} \\ & \Rightarrow a^{2}-2a+1+b^{2}-4b+4=\frac{8}{9} \\ & \Rightarrow a^{2}+b^{2}-2a-4b+5=\frac{8}{9} \\ & \Rightarrow 9a^{2}+9b^{2}-18a-36b+37=0 \end{aligned}$ Hence, $a=\frac{5}{3},b=\frac{4}{3}$ $\begin{aligned} & x_{1}y_{1}+x_{2}y_{2}+x_{3}y_{3}=2+ab+(2-a)(4-b) \\ & 9(x_{1}y_{1}+x_{2}y_{2}+x_{3}y_{3})=9(10+2ab-2b-4a) \\ & =90+18ab-18b-36a=46 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Solving the line $x+y=3$ , and the circle $x^{2}+$ $(y-1)^{2}=2$

Substitute $y=3-x$ :

$\begin{aligned} & x^{2}+(3-x-1)^{2}=2 \\ & \Rightarrow x^{2}-2x+1=0 \\ & \Rightarrow x=1 \Rightarrow y=2 \end{aligned}$

So, $P=(x_{1},y_{1})=(1,2) \Rightarrow x_{1}y_{1}=1 \cdot 2=2$

Use midpoint condition

Let $Q=(x_{2},y_{2}),R=(x_{3},y_{3})$ .

Since $P$ is the midpoint of QR:

$$x_2+x_3=2 x_1=2, y_2+y_3=2 y_1=4

$$So, we can write: $x_{3}=2-x_{2},y_{3}=4-y_{2}$

Given,

$PQ=\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} \Rightarrow PQ^{2}=(x_{2}-1)^{2}+(y_{2}-2)^{2}=\frac{8}{9}$

Let's denote: $x_{2}=a,y_{2}=b,x_{3}=2-a,y_{3}=4-b$

$\begin{aligned} & (a-1)^{2}+(b-2)^{2}=\frac{8}{9} \\ & \Rightarrow a^{2}-2a+1+b^{2}-4b+4=\frac{8}{9} \\ & \Rightarrow a^{2}+b^{2}-2a-4b+5=\frac{8}{9} \\ & \Rightarrow 9a^{2}+9b^{2}-18a-36b+37=0 \end{aligned}$

Hence, $a=\frac{5}{3},b=\frac{4}{3}$

$\begin{aligned} & x_{1}y_{1}+x_{2}y_{2}+x_{3}y_{3}=2+ab+(2-a)(4-b) \\ & 9(x_{1}y_{1}+x_{2}y_{2}+x_{3}y_{3})=9(10+2ab-2b-4a) \\ & =90+18ab-18b-36a=46 \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & 3x+5y=1 \\ & (2+c)x+5c^{2}y=1 \\ & 3c^{2}x+5c^{2}y=c^{2} \end{aligned}$ Subtracting $\begin{aligned} & (2+c-3c^{2})x=1-c^{2} \\ & x_{c}=\frac{1-c^{2}}{2+c-3c^{2}}=\frac{(1-c)(1+c)}{(1-c)(3c+2)}=\frac{c+1}{3c+2} \\ & y=\frac{1-3x}{5}=\frac{1-3(\frac{c+1}{3c+2})}{5} \\ & =\frac{3c+2-3c-3}{5(3c+2)} \\ & y_{c}=\frac{-1}{5(3c+2)} \\ & \underset{c \rightarrow 1}{lim}x_{c}=\frac{2}{5}=ℎ \\ & \underset{c \rightarrow 1}{lim}y_{c}=\frac{-1}{25}=k \end{aligned}$ Equation of circle is $25x^{2}+25y^{2}-20x+2y-60=0$
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & 3x+5y=1 \\ & (2+c)x+5c^{2}y=1 \\ & 3c^{2}x+5c^{2}y=c^{2} \end{aligned}$

Subtracting

$\begin{aligned} & (2+c-3c^{2})x=1-c^{2} \\ & x_{c}=\frac{1-c^{2}}{2+c-3c^{2}}=\frac{(1-c)(1+c)}{(1-c)(3c+2)}=\frac{c+1}{3c+2} \\ & y=\frac{1-3x}{5}=\frac{1-3(\frac{c+1}{3c+2})}{5} \\ & =\frac{3c+2-3c-3}{5(3c+2)} \\ & y_{c}=\frac{-1}{5(3c+2)} \\ & \underset{c \rightarrow 1}{lim}x_{c}=\frac{2}{5}=ℎ \\ & \underset{c \rightarrow 1}{lim}y_{c}=\frac{-1}{25}=k \end{aligned}$

Equation of circle is

$25x^{2}+25y^{2}-20x+2y-60=0$

Common chord is

also, this line intersects the $y$ -axis at the point

questions.explanation_text: One side of square is $y=x+k$ Distance of $(5,3)$ to the line $y=x+k$ is $\begin{aligned} & \frac{|3-5-k|}{\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{2} \\ & =|-2-k|=2 \\ & \Rightarrow k=0\text{or}k=-4 \end{aligned}$ So lines are $y=x$ and $y=x-4$ Now, solving these lines with circle $\begin{aligned} y= & x\text{and}x^{2}+y^{2}-10x-6y+30=0 \\ \Rightarrow & 2x^{2}-16x+30=0 \\ \Rightarrow & x=3,y=3 \\ & x=5,y=5 \\ & y=x-4\text{and}x^{2}+y^{2}-10x-6y+30=0 \\ \Rightarrow & x=5,y=1 \\ & x=7,y=3 \\ & \sum_{i=1}^{4}x_{i}^{2}+y_{i}^{2}=9+9+25+25+25+1+49+9 \\ = & 152 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{|3-5-k|}{\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{2} \\ & =|-2-k|=2 \\ & \Rightarrow k=0\text{or}k=-4 \end{aligned}$

So lines are $y=x$ and $y=x-4$

questions.question_html: Let the locus of the midpoints of the chords of the circle $x^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=1$ drawn from the origin intersect the line $x+y=1$ at $P$ and $Q$ . Then, the length of $PQ$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Let mid-point is $(x,y)$ $\begin{aligned} & x^{2}+y^{2}-2y=0 \\ \\ & xx_{1}+yy_{1}-(y+y_{1})=x_{1}^{2}+y_{1}^{2}-2y_{1} \end{aligned}$ It is passing through origin $\begin{aligned} & \text{So,}0+0-(0+y_{1})=x_{1}^{2}+y_{1}^{2}-2y_{1} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow -y_{1}=x_{1}^{2}+y_{1}^{2}-2y_{1} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x_{1}^{2}+y_{1}^{2}-y_{1}=0 \end{aligned}$ $x^{2}+y^{2}-y=0$ ............ (1) $\because$ It intersects the line $x+y=1$ So put $x=1-y$ in equation (1) $\begin{aligned} & (1-y)^{2}+y^{2}-y=0 \\ \\ & 2y^{2}-3y+1=0 \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow (y-1)(2y-1)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y=1,\frac{1}{2} \\ \\ & \therefore P(0,1)\text{and}Q(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}) \end{aligned}$ So, $PQ=\sqrt{(\frac{1}{2}-0)^{2}+(\frac{1}{2}-1)^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
questions.explanation_html:
Let mid-point is $(x,y)$

$\begin{aligned} & x^{2}+y^{2}-2y=0 \\ \\ & xx_{1}+yy_{1}-(y+y_{1})=x_{1}^{2}+y_{1}^{2}-2y_{1} \end{aligned}$

It is passing through origin

$\begin{aligned} & \text{So,}0+0-(0+y_{1})=x_{1}^{2}+y_{1}^{2}-2y_{1} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow -y_{1}=x_{1}^{2}+y_{1}^{2}-2y_{1} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x_{1}^{2}+y_{1}^{2}-y_{1}=0 \end{aligned}$

$x^{2}+y^{2}-y=0$ ............ (1)

$\because$ It intersects the line $x+y=1$

So put $x=1-y$ in equation (1)

$\begin{aligned} & (1-y)^{2}+y^{2}-y=0 \\ \\ & 2y^{2}-3y+1=0 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow (y-1)(2y-1)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow y=1,\frac{1}{2} \\ \\ & \therefore P(0,1)\text{and}Q(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}) \end{aligned}$

So, $PQ=\sqrt{(\frac{1}{2}-0)^{2}+(\frac{1}{2}-1)^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

questions.question_text: A line segment AB of length $\lambda$ moves such that the points A and B remain on the periphery of a circle of radius $\lambda$ . Then the locus of the point, that divides the line segment AB in the ratio 2 : 3, is a circle of radius :
questions.question_html: A line segment AB of length $\lambda$ moves such that the points A and B remain on the periphery of a circle of radius $\lambda$ . Then the locus of the point, that divides the line segment AB in the ratio 2 : 3, is a circle of radius :
questions.explanation_text: Given, length of $AB=\lambda$ So, $AC=\frac{\lambda}{2}$ and $AM=\frac{2\lambda}{5}$ $CM=AC-AM=\frac{\lambda}{2}-\frac{2\lambda}{5}=\frac{\lambda}{10}$ Now, from $△OCM$ , we get $\begin{aligned} & OM^{2}=CM^{2}+OC^{2} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}=(\frac{\lambda}{10})^{2}+(\lambda^{2}-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{4}) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}=\frac{\lambda^{2}}{100}+\frac{3\lambda^{2}}{4}=\frac{\lambda^{2}+75\lambda^{2}}{100} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}=\frac{76\lambda^{2}}{100}=\frac{19\lambda^{2}}{25} \\ \\ & \therefore x^{2}+y^{2}=(\frac{\sqrt{19}\lambda}{5})^{2} \end{aligned}$ So, radius is $\frac{\sqrt{19}\lambda}{5}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Given, length of $AB=\lambda$

So, $AC=\frac{\lambda}{2}$ and $AM=\frac{2\lambda}{5}$

$CM=AC-AM=\frac{\lambda}{2}-\frac{2\lambda}{5}=\frac{\lambda}{10}$



Now, from $△OCM$ , we get

$\begin{aligned} & OM^{2}=CM^{2}+OC^{2} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}=(\frac{\lambda}{10})^{2}+(\lambda^{2}-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{4}) \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}=\frac{\lambda^{2}}{100}+\frac{3\lambda^{2}}{4}=\frac{\lambda^{2}+75\lambda^{2}}{100} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}=\frac{76\lambda^{2}}{100}=\frac{19\lambda^{2}}{25} \\ \\ & \therefore x^{2}+y^{2}=(\frac{\sqrt{19}\lambda}{5})^{2} \end{aligned}$

So, radius is $\frac{\sqrt{19}\lambda}{5}$ .

questions.question_text: Let a circle $C_{1}$ be obtained on rolling the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-4x-6y+11=0$ upwards 4 units on the tangent $T$ to it at the point $(3,2)$ . Let $C_{2}$ be the image of $C_{1}$ in $T$ . Let $A$ and $B$ be the centers of circles $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ respectively, and $M$ and $N$ be respectively the feet of perpendiculars drawn from $A$ and $B$ on the $x$ -axis. Then the area of the trapezium AMNB is :
questions.question_html: Let a circle $C_{1}$ be obtained on rolling the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-4x-6y+11=0$ upwards 4 units on the tangent $T$ to it at the point $(3,2)$ . Let $C_{2}$ be the image of $C_{1}$ in $T$ . Let $A$ and $B$ be the centers of circles $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ respectively, and $M$ and $N$ be respectively the feet of perpendiculars drawn from $A$ and $B$ on the $x$ -axis. Then the area of the trapezium AMNB is :
questions.explanation_text: Given circle is $x^{2}+y^{2}-4x-6y+11=0$ , centre $(2,3)$ Tangent at $(3,2)$ is $x-y=1$ After rolling up by 4 units centre of $C_{1}$ is $A \equiv (2+\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}},3+\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}})$ $\Rightarrow A=(2+2\sqrt{2},3+2\sqrt{2})$ $B$ is the image of $A$ in $x-y=1$ $\frac{x-(2+2\sqrt{2})}{1}=\frac{y-(3+2\sqrt{2})}{-1}=\frac{-2(-2)}{2}=2$ $\Rightarrow x=4+2\sqrt{2},y=1+2\sqrt{2}$ Area of $AMNB$ $=\frac{1}{2}(4+4\sqrt{2})(4+2\sqrt{2}-(2+2\sqrt{2}))$ $=4(1+\sqrt{2})$
questions.explanation_html:
Given circle is $x^{2}+y^{2}-4x-6y+11=0$ , centre $(2,3)$

Tangent at $(3,2)$ is $x-y=1$

After rolling up by 4 units centre of $C_{1}$ is

$A \equiv (2+\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}},3+\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}})$

$\Rightarrow A=(2+2\sqrt{2},3+2\sqrt{2})$

$B$ is the image of $A$ in $x-y=1$

$\frac{x-(2+2\sqrt{2})}{1}=\frac{y-(3+2\sqrt{2})}{-1}=\frac{-2(-2)}{2}=2$

$\Rightarrow x=4+2\sqrt{2},y=1+2\sqrt{2}$

Area of $AMNB$

$=\frac{1}{2}(4+4\sqrt{2})(4+2\sqrt{2}-(2+2\sqrt{2}))$

$=4(1+\sqrt{2})$

If $\theta_{1}=\frac{\pi}{3},\theta_{3}=\frac{2\pi}{3}$ and $r_{1}^{2}=r_{2}^{2}+r_{3}^{2}$ , then $\theta_{2}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $\therefore cos(\frac{\theta_{1}}{2})=\frac{r_{i}}{2} \Rightarrow r_{i}=2cos(\frac{\theta_{i}}{2})$ Given $r_{1}^{2}=r_{2}^{2}+r_{3}^{3}$ $\Rightarrow (cos(\frac{\theta_{1}}{2}))^{2}=(cos(\frac{\theta_{2}}{2}))^{2}+(cos(\frac{\theta_{3}}{2}))^{2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{3}{4}=cos^{2}(\frac{\theta_{2}}{2})+\frac{1}{4}$ $\Rightarrow cos^{2}(\frac{\theta_{2}}{2})=\frac{1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{\theta_{2}}{2}=\frac{\pi}{4}$ $\Rightarrow \theta_{2}=\frac{\pi}{2}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\therefore cos(\frac{\theta_{1}}{2})=\frac{r_{i}}{2} \Rightarrow r_{i}=2cos(\frac{\theta_{i}}{2})$

Given $r_{1}^{2}=r_{2}^{2}+r_{3}^{3}$

A circle passing through the point $P(\alpha,\beta)$ in the first quadrant touches the two coordinate axes at the points $A$ and $B$ . The point $P$ is above the line $AB$ . The point $Q$ on the line segment $AB$ is the foot of perpendicular from $P$ on $AB$ . If $PQ$ is equal to 11 units, then the value of $\alpha\beta$ is
 ___________.
questions.question_html: A circle passing through the point $P(\alpha,\beta)$ in the first quadrant touches the two coordinate axes at the points $A$ and $B$ . The point $P$ is above the line $AB$ . The point $Q$ on the line segment $AB$ is the foot of perpendicular from $P$ on $AB$ . If $PQ$ is equal to 11 units, then the value of $\alpha\beta$ is ___________.
questions.explanation_text: Let equation of circle is $(x-a)^{2}+(y-a)^{2}=a^{2}$ Since, (i) passes through $P(\alpha,\beta)$ $\therefore (\alpha-a)^{2}+(\beta-a)^{2}=a^{2}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}-2\alpha a-2\beta a+a^{2}=0.........(i) \end{aligned}$ Equation of $AB=\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{a}=1$ $\Rightarrow x+y=a$ .........(ii) Let $Q(p,q)$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to line (iii) $\begin{aligned} & \therefore \frac{p-\alpha}{1}=\frac{q-\beta}{1}=\frac{-(\alpha+\beta-\alpha)}{(1)^{2}+(1)^{2}} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{p-\alpha}{1}=\frac{q-\beta}{1}=\frac{-(\alpha+\beta-a)}{2} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow p-\alpha=\frac{-(\alpha+\beta-a)}{2} \\ \\ & \text{and}q-\beta=\frac{-(\alpha+\beta-a)}{2} \end{aligned}$ Now, $\begin{aligned} & PQ^{2}=(p-\alpha)^{2}+(q-\beta)^{2} \\ \\ & =\frac{1}{4}(\alpha+\beta-a)^{2}+\frac{1}{4}(\alpha+\beta-a)^{2} \end{aligned}$ $\Rightarrow (11)^{2}=\frac{1}{2}(\alpha+\beta-\alpha)^{2}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+a^{2}+2\alpha\beta-2\beta a-2\alpha a=242 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 2\alpha\beta=242\text{[Using Eq. (ii)]} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha\beta=121 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Let equation of circle is $(x-a)^{2}+(y-a)^{2}=a^{2}$

Since, (i) passes through $P(\alpha,\beta)$



$\therefore (\alpha-a)^{2}+(\beta-a)^{2}=a^{2}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}-2\alpha a-2\beta a+a^{2}=0.........(i) \end{aligned}$

Equation of $AB=\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{a}=1$

$\Rightarrow x+y=a$ .........(ii)

Let $Q(p,q)$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to line (iii)

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \frac{p-\alpha}{1}=\frac{q-\beta}{1}=\frac{-(\alpha+\beta-\alpha)}{(1)^{2}+(1)^{2}} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{p-\alpha}{1}=\frac{q-\beta}{1}=\frac{-(\alpha+\beta-a)}{2} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow p-\alpha=\frac{-(\alpha+\beta-a)}{2} \\ \\ & \text{and}q-\beta=\frac{-(\alpha+\beta-a)}{2} \end{aligned}$

Now,

$\begin{aligned} & PQ^{2}=(p-\alpha)^{2}+(q-\beta)^{2} \\ \\ & =\frac{1}{4}(\alpha+\beta-a)^{2}+\frac{1}{4}(\alpha+\beta-a)^{2} \end{aligned}$

$\Rightarrow (11)^{2}=\frac{1}{2}(\alpha+\beta-\alpha)^{2}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+a^{2}+2\alpha\beta-2\beta a-2\alpha a=242 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 2\alpha\beta=242\text{[Using Eq. (ii)]} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha\beta=121 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: The number of common tangents, to the circles $x^{2}+y^{2}-18x-15y+131=0$ and $x^{2}+y^{2}-6x-6y-7=0$ , is :
questions.question_html:
The number of common tangents, to the circles

$x^{2}+y^{2}-18x-15y+131=0$

and $x^{2}+y^{2}-6x-6y-7=0$ , is :
questions.explanation_text: We are given two circles: (1) $x^{2}+y^{2}-18x-15y+131=0$ (2) $x^{2}+y^{2}-6x-6y-7=0$ First, let's find the centers and radii of the circles. For circle (1): Completing the square for the equation: $(x^{2}-18x+81)+(y^{2}-15y+\frac{225}{4})=-131+81+\frac{225}{4}$ $(x-9)^{2}+(y-\frac{15}{2})^{2}=\frac{25}{4}$ Center 1: $C_{1}(9,\frac{15}{2})$ Radius 1: $r_{1}=\sqrt{\frac{25}{4}}=\frac{5}{2}$ For circle (2): Completing the square for the equation: $(x^{2}-6x+9)+(y^{2}-6y+9)=7+9+9$ $(x-3)^{2}+(y-3)^{2}=25$ Center 2: $C_{2}(3,3)$ Radius 2: $r_{2}=5$ Now, let's find the distance between the centers : $d=\sqrt{(9-3)^{2}+(\frac{15}{2}-3)^{2}}=\sqrt{6^{2}+\frac{9}{2}^{2}}=\sqrt{36+\frac{81}{4}}=\frac{15}{2}$ Next, let's analyze the relative positions of the circles using the distance between centers and the sum and difference of the radii : If $d>r_{1}+r_{2}$ , the circles are separate, and there are 4 common tangents. If $d=r_{1}+r_{2}$ , the circles are externally tangent, and there are 3 common tangents. If $0<d<|r_{1}-r_{2}|$ , one circle is inside the other, and there are no common tangents. If $d=|r_{1}-r_{2}|$ , the circles are internally tangent, and there is 1 common tangent. If $d<|r_{1}-r_{2}|$ , one circle is completely inside the other, and there are no common tangents. In this case : $d=\frac{15}{2}$ $r_{1}=\frac{5}{2}$ $r_{2}=5$ Now, let's check the conditions : $r_{1}+r_{2}=\frac{5}{2}+5$ = $\frac{15}{2}$ Since $d=\frac{15}{2}=r_{1}+r_{2}$ , the circles touch each other externally, and there are 3 common tangents.
questions.explanation_html:
We are given two circles:

(1) $x^{2}+y^{2}-18x-15y+131=0$

(2) $x^{2}+y^{2}-6x-6y-7=0$

First, let's find the centers and radii of the circles.

For circle (1):

Completing the square for the equation:

$(x^{2}-18x+81)+(y^{2}-15y+\frac{225}{4})=-131+81+\frac{225}{4}$

$(x-9)^{2}+(y-\frac{15}{2})^{2}=\frac{25}{4}$

Center 1: $C_{1}(9,\frac{15}{2})$

Radius 1: $r_{1}=\sqrt{\frac{25}{4}}=\frac{5}{2}$

For circle (2):

Completing the square for the equation:

$(x^{2}-6x+9)+(y^{2}-6y+9)=7+9+9$

$(x-3)^{2}+(y-3)^{2}=25$

Center 2: $C_{2}(3,3)$

Radius 2: $r_{2}=5$

Now, let's find the distance between the centers :

$d=\sqrt{(9-3)^{2}+(\frac{15}{2}-3)^{2}}=\sqrt{6^{2}+\frac{9}{2}^{2}}=\sqrt{36+\frac{81}{4}}=\frac{15}{2}$

Next, let's analyze the relative positions of the circles using the distance between centers and the sum and difference of the radii :

  1. If $d>r_{1}+r_{2}$ , the circles are separate, and there are 4 common tangents.
  2. If $d=r_{1}+r_{2}$ , the circles are externally tangent, and there are 3 common tangents.
  3. If $0<d<|r_{1}-r_{2}|$ , one circle is inside the other, and there are no common tangents.
  4. If $d=|r_{1}-r_{2}|$ , the circles are internally tangent, and there is 1 common tangent.
  5. If $d<|r_{1}-r_{2}|$ , one circle is completely inside the other, and there are no common tangents.

In this case :

$d=\frac{15}{2}$

$r_{1}=\frac{5}{2}$

$r_{2}=5$

Now, let's check the conditions :

$r_{1}+r_{2}=\frac{5}{2}+5$ = $\frac{15}{2}$

Since $d=\frac{15}{2}=r_{1}+r_{2}$ , the circles touch each other externally, and there are 3 common tangents.

questions.question_text: Let O be the origin and OP and OQ be the tangents to the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-6x+4y+8=0$ at the points P and Q on it. If the circumcircle of the triangle OPQ passes through the point $(\alpha,\frac{1}{2})$ , then a value of $\alpha$ is :
questions.question_html: Let O be the origin and OP and OQ be the tangents to the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-6x+4y+8=0$ at the points P and Q on it. If the circumcircle of the triangle OPQ passes through the point $(\alpha,\frac{1}{2})$ , then a value of $\alpha$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Centre $(3,-2)$ Equation of circumcircle is $\begin{aligned} & x(x-3)+y(y+2)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x^{2}-3x+y^{2}+2y=0 \end{aligned}$ Since $(\alpha,\frac{1}{2})$ is on the circle $\begin{aligned} & \text{So}\alpha^{2}-3\alpha+\frac{1}{4}+1=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 4\alpha^{2}-12\alpha+5=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{12 \pm \sqrt{144-80}}{8} \\ \\ & =\frac{12 \pm \sqrt{64}}{8}=\frac{12 \pm 8}{8} \\ \\ & \alpha=\frac{20}{8},\frac{4}{8}=\frac{5}{2},\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Centre $(3,-2)$

Equation of circumcircle is

$\begin{aligned} & x(x-3)+y(y+2)=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x^{2}-3x+y^{2}+2y=0 \end{aligned}$

Since $(\alpha,\frac{1}{2})$ is on the circle

$\begin{aligned} & \text{So}\alpha^{2}-3\alpha+\frac{1}{4}+1=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 4\alpha^{2}-12\alpha+5=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{12 \pm \sqrt{144-80}}{8} \\ \\ & =\frac{12 \pm \sqrt{64}}{8}=\frac{12 \pm 8}{8} \\ \\ & \alpha=\frac{20}{8},\frac{4}{8}=\frac{5}{2},\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Two circles in the first quadrant of radii $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ touch the coordinate axes. Each of them cuts off an intercept of 2 units with the line $x+y=2$ . Then $r_{1}^{2}+r_{2}^{2}-r_{1}r_{2}$ is equal to ___________.
questions.question_html: Two circles in the first quadrant of radii $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ touch the coordinate axes. Each of them cuts off an intercept of 2 units with the line $x+y=2$ . Then $r_{1}^{2}+r_{2}^{2}-r_{1}r_{2}$ is equal to ___________.
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & \text{Circle}(x-a)^{2}+(y-a)^{2}=a^{2} \\ \\ & x^{2}+y^{2}-2ax-2ay+a^{2}=0 \\ \\ & \text{intercept}=2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 2\sqrt{a^{2}-d^{2}}=2 \end{aligned}$ Where $d=$ perpendicular distance of centre from line $x+y=2$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow 2\sqrt{a^{2}-(\frac{a+a-2}{\sqrt{2}})^{2}}=2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow a^{2}-\frac{(2a-2)^{2}}{2}=1 \Rightarrow 2a^{2}-4a^{2}+8a-4=2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 2a^{2}-8a+6=0 \Rightarrow a^{2}-4a+3=0 \\ \\ & \therefore r_{1}+r_{2}=4\text{and}r_{1}r_{2}=3 \\ \\ & \therefore r_{1}^{2}+r_{2}^{2}-r_{1}r_{2}=(r_{1}+r_{2})^{2}-3r_{1}r_{2} \\ \\ & =16-9=7 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & \text{Circle}(x-a)^{2}+(y-a)^{2}=a^{2} \\ \\ & x^{2}+y^{2}-2ax-2ay+a^{2}=0 \\ \\ & \text{intercept}=2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 2\sqrt{a^{2}-d^{2}}=2 \end{aligned}$



Where $d=$ perpendicular distance of centre from line $x+y=2$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow 2\sqrt{a^{2}-(\frac{a+a-2}{\sqrt{2}})^{2}}=2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow a^{2}-\frac{(2a-2)^{2}}{2}=1 \Rightarrow 2a^{2}-4a^{2}+8a-4=2 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 2a^{2}-8a+6=0 \Rightarrow a^{2}-4a+3=0 \\ \\ & \therefore r_{1}+r_{2}=4\text{and}r_{1}r_{2}=3 \\ \\ & \therefore r_{1}^{2}+r_{2}^{2}-r_{1}r_{2}=(r_{1}+r_{2})^{2}-3r_{1}r_{2} \\ \\ & =16-9=7 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let $P(a_{1},b_{1})$ and $Q(a_{2},b_{2})$ be two distinct points on a circle with center $C(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{3})$ . Let $O$ be the origin and $OC$ be perpendicular to both $CP$ and $CQ$ . If the area of the triangle $OCP$ is $\frac{\sqrt{35}}{2}$ , then $a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}+b_{1}^{2}+b_{2}^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let $P(a_{1},b_{1})$ and $Q(a_{2},b_{2})$ be two distinct points on a circle with center $C(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{3})$ . Let $O$ be the origin and $OC$ be perpendicular to both $CP$ and $CQ$ . If the area of the triangle $OCP$ is $\frac{\sqrt{35}}{2}$ , then $a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}+b_{1}^{2}+b_{2}^{2}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_html:
$OC\perpCP$ and $OC\perpCQ$

$\Rightarrow PCQ$ is a straight line

$OC=\sqrt{(\sqrt{2})^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}=\sqrt{5}$

Let $CP=CQ=I$

$[OCP]=\frac{1}{2} \times OC \times I=\frac{\sqrt{35}}{2}$

$I=\sqrt{7}$

$OP=OQ=\sqrt{(OC)^{2}+I^{2}}=\sqrt{5+7}=\sqrt{12}$

$a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}+b_{1}^{2}+b_{2}^{2}=(a_{1}^{2}+b_{2}^{2})+(a_{2}^{2}+b_{2}^{2})$

$OP^{2}+OQ^{2}=12+12=24$

questions.question_text: Let the centre of a circle C be $(\alpha,\beta)$ and its radius $r<8$ . Let $3x+4y=24$ and $3x-4y=32$ be two tangents and $4x+3y=1$ be a normal to C. Then $(\alpha-\beta+r)$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let the centre of a circle C be $(\alpha,\beta)$ and its radius $r<8$ . Let $3x+4y=24$ and $3x-4y=32$ be two tangents and $4x+3y=1$ be a normal to C. Then $(\alpha-\beta+r)$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: First find point A by solving $4x+3y=1$ and $3x-4y=32$ After solving, point $A$ is $(4,-5)$ Centre $(\alpha,\beta)$ lie on $4x+3y=1$ $4\alpha+3\beta=1 \Rightarrow \beta=\frac{1-4\alpha}{3}$ Now distance from centre to line $3x-4y-32=$ 0 and $3x+4y-24=0$ are equal. $|\frac{3\alpha-4(\frac{1-4\alpha}{3})-32}{5}|=|\frac{3\alpha+4(\frac{1-4\alpha}{3})-24}{5}|$ After solving $\alpha=1$ and $\alpha=\frac{28}{3}$ For $\alpha=1$ , centre $(1,-1) \Rightarrow$ radius $=5$ For $\alpha=\frac{28}{3}$ , centre $(\frac{28}{3},\frac{-109}{2})$ $\Rightarrow \text{radius} \approx 49.78\text{(rejected})$ Hence, $\alpha=1,\beta=-1,r=5$ $\alpha-\beta+r=7$
questions.explanation_html:
First find point A by solving $4x+3y=1$ and $3x-4y=32$

After solving, point $A$ is $(4,-5)$

Centre $(\alpha,\beta)$ lie on $4x+3y=1$

$4\alpha+3\beta=1 \Rightarrow \beta=\frac{1-4\alpha}{3}$

Now distance from centre to line $3x-4y-32=$ 0 and $3x+4y-24=0$ are equal.

$|\frac{3\alpha-4(\frac{1-4\alpha}{3})-32}{5}|=|\frac{3\alpha+4(\frac{1-4\alpha}{3})-24}{5}|$

After solving $\alpha=1$ and $\alpha=\frac{28}{3}$

For $\alpha=1$ , centre $(1,-1) \Rightarrow$ radius $=5$

For $\alpha=\frac{28}{3}$ , centre $(\frac{28}{3},\frac{-109}{2})$

$\Rightarrow \text{radius} \approx 49.78\text{(rejected})$

Hence, $\alpha=1,\beta=-1,r=5$

$\alpha-\beta+r=7$

questions.question_text: If the tangents at the points $P$ and $Q$ on the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-2x+y=5$ meet at the point $R(\frac{9}{4},2)$ , then the area of the triangle $PQR$ is :
questions.question_html: If the tangents at the points $P$ and $Q$ on the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-2x+y=5$ meet at the point $R(\frac{9}{4},2)$ , then the area of the triangle $PQR$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Equation of circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-2x+y-5=0$ On comparing with $x^{2}+y^{2}+2gx+2fy+c=0$ $\begin{aligned} 2g=-2,2f=1,c=-5 \\ \\ g=-1,f=\frac{1}{2},c=-5 \end{aligned}$ $\therefore$ Radius of the circle $r=\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(\frac{1}{2})^{2}+5}=\frac{5}{2}$ Length of tangent, $PR=\sqrt{S_{1}}$ $l=\sqrt{(\frac{9}{4})^{2}+(2)^{2}-2(\frac{9}{4})+2-5}=\frac{5}{4}$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore \text{Area of}△PQR=\frac{rl^{3}}{r^{2}+l^{2}} \\ \\ & =\frac{(\frac{5}{2})(\frac{5}{4})^{3}}{(\frac{5}{2})^{2}+(\frac{5}{4})^{2}}=\frac{\frac{5}{2} \times \frac{125}{64}}{\frac{25}{4}+\frac{25}{16}} \\ \\ & =\frac{\frac{5}{2} \times \frac{125}{64} \times 16}{125}=\frac{5}{8} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-2x+y-5=0$

On comparing with $x^{2}+y^{2}+2gx+2fy+c=0$

$\begin{aligned} 2g=-2,2f=1,c=-5 \\ \\ g=-1,f=\frac{1}{2},c=-5 \end{aligned}$

$\therefore$ Radius of the circle

$r=\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(\frac{1}{2})^{2}+5}=\frac{5}{2}$



Length of tangent, $PR=\sqrt{S_{1}}$

$l=\sqrt{(\frac{9}{4})^{2}+(2)^{2}-2(\frac{9}{4})+2-5}=\frac{5}{4}$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \text{Area of}△PQR=\frac{rl^{3}}{r^{2}+l^{2}} \\ \\ & =\frac{(\frac{5}{2})(\frac{5}{4})^{3}}{(\frac{5}{2})^{2}+(\frac{5}{4})^{2}}=\frac{\frac{5}{2} \times \frac{125}{64}}{\frac{25}{4}+\frac{25}{16}} \\ \\ & =\frac{\frac{5}{2} \times \frac{125}{64} \times 16}{125}=\frac{5}{8} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let the tangents at the points $A(4,-11)$ and $B(8,-5)$ on the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-3x+10y-15=0$ , intersect at the point $C$ . Then the radius of the circle, whose centre is $C$ and the line joining $A$ and $B$ is its tangent, is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let the tangents at the points $A(4,-11)$ and $B(8,-5)$ on the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-3x+10y-15=0$ , intersect at the point $C$ . Then the radius of the circle, whose centre is $C$ and the line joining $A$ and $B$ is its tangent, is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Equation of AB : $y-(-5)=\frac{-5+11}{8-4}(x-8)$ $\Rightarrow y+5=\frac{3}{2}(x-8)$ $\Rightarrow 2y+10=3x-24$ $\Rightarrow 3x-2y-34=0$ .... (1) Also AB is cord of contact. And we know equation of cord of contact to a circle is $T=0$ $\Rightarrow xℎ+yk-\frac{3}{2}(x+ℎ)+5(y+k)-15=0$ $\Rightarrow x(ℎ-\frac{3}{2})+y(k+5)+(-\frac{3}{2}ℎ+5k-15)=0$ .... (2) Comparing equation (1) and (2), we get $\frac{ℎ-\frac{3}{2}}{3}=\frac{k+5}{-2}=\frac{-\frac{3}{2}ℎ+5k-15}{-34}$ $\therefore$ $-2ℎ+3=3k+15$ $\Rightarrow 3k+2ℎ=-12$ ..... (3) and $17(k+5)=-\frac{3}{2}ℎ+5k-15$ $\Rightarrow 12k+\frac{3}{2}ℎ-100$ $\Rightarrow 3ℎ+24k=-200$ ..... (4) Solving (3) and (4), we get $ℎ=8$ and $k=-\frac{28}{3}$ $\therefore$ Point C is $(8,-\frac{28}{3})$ Now radius of the circle whose centre is at C and tangent is AB is $=|\frac{3(8)-2(-\frac{28}{3})-34}{\sqrt{3^{2}+2^{2}}}|$ $=|\frac{26}{3\sqrt{13}}|$ $=\frac{2\sqrt{13}}{3}$
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of AB :

$y-(-5)=\frac{-5+11}{8-4}(x-8)$

$\Rightarrow y+5=\frac{3}{2}(x-8)$

$\Rightarrow 2y+10=3x-24$

$\Rightarrow 3x-2y-34=0$ .... (1)

Also AB is cord of contact. And we know equation of cord of contact to a circle is $T=0$

$\Rightarrow xℎ+yk-\frac{3}{2}(x+ℎ)+5(y+k)-15=0$

$\Rightarrow x(ℎ-\frac{3}{2})+y(k+5)+(-\frac{3}{2}ℎ+5k-15)=0$ .... (2)

Comparing equation (1) and (2), we get

$\frac{ℎ-\frac{3}{2}}{3}=\frac{k+5}{-2}=\frac{-\frac{3}{2}ℎ+5k-15}{-34}$

$\therefore$ $-2ℎ+3=3k+15$

$\Rightarrow 3k+2ℎ=-12$ ..... (3)

and

$17(k+5)=-\frac{3}{2}ℎ+5k-15$

$\Rightarrow 12k+\frac{3}{2}ℎ-100$

$\Rightarrow 3ℎ+24k=-200$ ..... (4)

Solving (3) and (4), we get

$ℎ=8$ and $k=-\frac{28}{3}$

$\therefore$ Point C is $(8,-\frac{28}{3})$

Now radius of the circle whose centre is at C and tangent is AB is

$=|\frac{3(8)-2(-\frac{28}{3})-34}{\sqrt{3^{2}+2^{2}}}|$

$=|\frac{26}{3\sqrt{13}}|$

$=\frac{2\sqrt{13}}{3}$

questions.question_text: Consider a circle $C_{1}:x^{2}+y^{2}-4x-2y=\alpha-5$ . Let its mirror image in the line $y=2x+1$ be another circle $C_{2}:5x^{2}+5y^{2}-10fx-10gy+36=0$ . Let $r$ be the radius of $C_{2}$ . Then $\alpha+r$ is equal to _________.
questions.question_html: Consider a circle $C_{1}:x^{2}+y^{2}-4x-2y=\alpha-5$ . Let its mirror image in the line $y=2x+1$ be another circle $C_{2}:5x^{2}+5y^{2}-10fx-10gy+36=0$ . Let $r$ be the radius of $C_{2}$ . Then $\alpha+r$ is equal to _________.
questions.explanation_text: We have, $\begin{aligned} & C_{1}:x^{2}+y^{2}-4x-2y=\alpha-5 \\ \\ & C_{1}:(x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{5}-5=\alpha-5 \\ \\ & C_{1}:(x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=(\sqrt{\alpha})^{2} \end{aligned}$ So, centre and radius of $C_{1}$ are $(2,1)$ and $\sqrt{\alpha}$ respectively Now, image of $(2,1)$ along the line $y=2x+1$ is, $\frac{x-2}{2}=\frac{y-1}{-1}=\frac{-2(4-1+1)}{2^{2}+(-1)^{2}}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{x-2}{2}=\frac{y-1}{-1}=\frac{-8}{5} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x=\frac{-6}{5}\text{and}y=\frac{13}{5} \end{aligned}$ Now, $(\frac{-6}{5},\frac{13}{5})$ will be the centre of $C_{2}$ $\therefore f=\frac{6}{5}\text{and}g=\frac{-13}{5}$ Now, radius of $C_{2}=r=\sqrt{f^{2}+g^{2}-\frac{36}{5}}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow r=\sqrt{\frac{36}{25}+\frac{169}{25}-\frac{36}{5}}=1 \\ \\ & \because r=1\text{so,}\alpha=1 \\ \\ & \therefore \alpha+r=1+1=2 \end{aligned}$ Concept : Image of a point $(x_{1},y_{1})$ w.r.t. $ax+by+c=0$ is $(x,y)$ , then $\frac{x-x_{1}}{a}=\frac{y-y_{1}}{b}=\frac{-2(ax_{1}+by_{1}+c)}{(a^{2}+b^{2})}$
questions.explanation_html:
We have,

$\begin{aligned} & C_{1}:x^{2}+y^{2}-4x-2y=\alpha-5 \\ \\ & C_{1}:(x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{5}-5=\alpha-5 \\ \\ & C_{1}:(x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=(\sqrt{\alpha})^{2} \end{aligned}$

So, centre and radius of $C_{1}$ are $(2,1)$ and $\sqrt{\alpha}$ respectively

Now, image of $(2,1)$ along the line $y=2x+1$ is,

$\frac{x-2}{2}=\frac{y-1}{-1}=\frac{-2(4-1+1)}{2^{2}+(-1)^{2}}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{x-2}{2}=\frac{y-1}{-1}=\frac{-8}{5} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x=\frac{-6}{5}\text{and}y=\frac{13}{5} \end{aligned}$

Now, $(\frac{-6}{5},\frac{13}{5})$ will be the centre of $C_{2}$

$\therefore f=\frac{6}{5}\text{and}g=\frac{-13}{5}$

Now, radius of $C_{2}=r=\sqrt{f^{2}+g^{2}-\frac{36}{5}}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow r=\sqrt{\frac{36}{25}+\frac{169}{25}-\frac{36}{5}}=1 \\ \\ & \because r=1\text{so,}\alpha=1 \\ \\ & \therefore \alpha+r=1+1=2 \end{aligned}$

Concept :

Image of a point $(x_{1},y_{1})$ w.r.t. $ax+by+c=0$ is $(x,y)$ , then

$\frac{x-x_{1}}{a}=\frac{y-y_{1}}{b}=\frac{-2(ax_{1}+by_{1}+c)}{(a^{2}+b^{2})}$

questions.question_text: A circle with centre (2, 3) and radius 4 intersects the line $x+y=3$ at the points P and Q. If the tangents at P and Q intersect at the point $S(\alpha,\beta)$ , then $4\alpha-7\beta$ is equal to ___________.
questions.question_html: A circle with centre (2, 3) and radius 4 intersects the line $x+y=3$ at the points P and Q. If the tangents at P and Q intersect at the point $S(\alpha,\beta)$ , then $4\alpha-7\beta$ is equal to ___________.
questions.explanation_text: The line $x+y=3$ ..... (i) is polar of $S(\alpha,\beta)$ w.r.t. circle $(x-2)^{2}+(y-3)^{2}=16$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}-4x-6y-3=0$ Equation of polar is $\alpha x+\beta y-2(x+\alpha)-3(4+\beta)-3=0$ $(\alpha-2)x+(\alpha-3)y-(2\alpha+3\beta+3)=0$ ..... (ii) (i) and (ii) represent the same. $\therefore$ $\frac{\alpha-2}{1}=\frac{\beta-3}{1}=\frac{2\alpha+3\beta+3}{3}$ $\alpha-\beta+1=0$ $\alpha-3\beta-9=0$ $\Rightarrow \alpha=-6,\beta=-5$ $4\alpha-7\beta=11$
questions.explanation_html:
The line $x+y=3$ ..... (i)

is polar of $S(\alpha,\beta)$ w.r.t. circle

$(x-2)^{2}+(y-3)^{2}=16$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}-4x-6y-3=0$

Equation of polar is

$\alpha x+\beta y-2(x+\alpha)-3(4+\beta)-3=0$

$(\alpha-2)x+(\alpha-3)y-(2\alpha+3\beta+3)=0$ ..... (ii)

(i) and (ii) represent the same.

$\therefore$ $\frac{\alpha-2}{1}=\frac{\beta-3}{1}=\frac{2\alpha+3\beta+3}{3}$

$\alpha-\beta+1=0$

$\alpha-3\beta-9=0$

$\Rightarrow \alpha=-6,\beta=-5$

$4\alpha-7\beta=11$

questions.question_text: Let A be the point $(1,2)$ and B be any point on the curve $x^{2}+y^{2}=16$ . If the centre of the locus of the point P, which divides the line segment $AB$ in the ratio $3:2$ is the point C $(\alpha,\beta)$ , then the length of the line segment $AC$ is :
questions.question_html: Let A be the point $(1,2)$ and B be any point on the curve $x^{2}+y^{2}=16$ . If the centre of the locus of the point P, which divides the line segment $AB$ in the ratio $3:2$ is the point C $(\alpha,\beta)$ , then the length of the line segment $AC$ is :
questions.explanation_text: We have, equation of circle is $x^{2}+y^{2}=16$ Let any point on the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=4^{2}$ is $B(4cos\theta,4sin\theta)$ and $A(1,2)$ Let $P$ be $(ℎ,k)$ which divides $AB$ in $3:2$ So $ℎ=\frac{12cos\theta+2}{3+2}\text{and}k=\frac{12sin\theta+2 \times 2}{3+2}$ $\Rightarrow cos\theta=\frac{5ℎ-2}{12}$ and $sin\theta=\frac{5k-4}{12}$ As, $cos^{2}\theta+sin^{2}\theta=1,(\frac{5ℎ-2}{12})^{2}+(\frac{5k-4}{12})^{2}=1$ $\Rightarrow (ℎ-\frac{2}{5})^{2}+(k-\frac{4}{5})^{2}=\frac{12^{2}}{5^{2}}$ $\therefore$ Locus of point $P$ is $(x-\frac{2}{5})^{2}+(y-\frac{4}{5})^{2}=\frac{12^{2}}{5^{2}}$ which is equation of circle with centre $(\frac{2}{5},\frac{4}{5})$ Hence, $AC=\sqrt{(1-\frac{2}{5})^{2}+(2-\frac{4}{5})^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{45}}{5}=\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{5}$
questions.explanation_html:
We have, equation of circle is $x^{2}+y^{2}=16$

Let any point on the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=4^{2}$ is $B(4cos\theta,4sin\theta)$ and $A(1,2)$

Let $P$ be $(ℎ,k)$ which divides $AB$ in $3:2$



So

$ℎ=\frac{12cos\theta+2}{3+2}\text{and}k=\frac{12sin\theta+2 \times 2}{3+2}$

$\Rightarrow cos\theta=\frac{5ℎ-2}{12}$ and $sin\theta=\frac{5k-4}{12}$

As, $cos^{2}\theta+sin^{2}\theta=1,(\frac{5ℎ-2}{12})^{2}+(\frac{5k-4}{12})^{2}=1$

$\Rightarrow (ℎ-\frac{2}{5})^{2}+(k-\frac{4}{5})^{2}=\frac{12^{2}}{5^{2}}$

$\therefore$ Locus of point $P$ is $(x-\frac{2}{5})^{2}+(y-\frac{4}{5})^{2}=\frac{12^{2}}{5^{2}}$

which is equation of circle with centre $(\frac{2}{5},\frac{4}{5})$

Hence, $AC=\sqrt{(1-\frac{2}{5})^{2}+(2-\frac{4}{5})^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{45}}{5}=\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{5}$

questions.question_text: The set of all values of $a^{2}$ for which the line $x+y=0$ bisects two distinct chords drawn from a point $P(\frac{1+a}{2},\frac{1-a}{2})$ on the circle $2x^{2}+2y^{2}-(1+a)x-(1-a)y=0$ , is equal to :
questions.question_html: The set of all values of $a^{2}$ for which the line $x+y=0$ bisects two distinct chords drawn from a point $P(\frac{1+a}{2},\frac{1-a}{2})$ on the circle $2x^{2}+2y^{2}-(1+a)x-(1-a)y=0$ , is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $x^{2}+y^{2}-\frac{(1+a)x}{2}-\frac{(1-a)y}{2}=0$ Centre $(\frac{1+a}{4},\frac{1-a}{4}) \Rightarrow (h,k)$ $P(\frac{1+a}{2},\frac{1-a}{2}) \Rightarrow (2h,2k)$ Equation of chord $\Rightarrow T=S_{1}$ $\Rightarrow (x-y)\lambda-\frac{2h(x+\lambda)}{2}-\frac{(2k)(y-\lambda)}{2}$ $=2\lambda^{2}-2h(\lambda)+2k\lambda$ Now, $\lambda(2h,2k)$ satisfies the chord $\therefore (2h-2k)\lambda-h(x+\lambda)-k(y-\lambda)$ $\Rightarrow 2\lambda^{2}+4k\lambda-4h\lambda+h\lambda-k\lambda+hx+ky=0$ $\Rightarrow 2\lambda^{2}+\lambda(3k-3h)+ky+hx=0$ $\Rightarrow D>0$ $\Rightarrow 9(k-h)^{2}-8(ky+hx)>0$ $\Rightarrow 9(k-h)^{2}-8(2k^{2}+2h^{2})>0$ $\Rightarrow -7k^{2}-7h^{2}-18kh>0$ $\Rightarrow 7k^{2}+7h^{2}+18kh<0$ $\Rightarrow 7(\frac{1-a}{4})^{2}+7(\frac{1+a}{4})^{2}+18(\frac{1-a^{2}}{16})<0$ $\Rightarrow 7[\frac{2(1+a^{2})}{16}]+\frac{18(1-a^{2})}{16}<0,a^{2}=t$ $\Rightarrow \frac{7}{8}(1+t)+\frac{18(1-t)}{16}<0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{14+14t+18-18t}{16}<0$ $\Rightarrow 4t>32$ $\Rightarrow$ $t>8$ $\Rightarrow$ $a^{2}>8$
questions.explanation_html:
$x^{2}+y^{2}-\frac{(1+a)x}{2}-\frac{(1-a)y}{2}=0$

Centre $(\frac{1+a}{4},\frac{1-a}{4}) \Rightarrow (h,k)$

$P(\frac{1+a}{2},\frac{1-a}{2}) \Rightarrow (2h,2k)$


Equation of chord $\Rightarrow T=S_{1}$

$\Rightarrow (x-y)\lambda-\frac{2h(x+\lambda)}{2}-\frac{(2k)(y-\lambda)}{2}$

$=2\lambda^{2}-2h(\lambda)+2k\lambda$

Now, $\lambda(2h,2k)$ satisfies the chord

$\therefore (2h-2k)\lambda-h(x+\lambda)-k(y-\lambda)$

$\Rightarrow 2\lambda^{2}+4k\lambda-4h\lambda+h\lambda-k\lambda+hx+ky=0$

$\Rightarrow 2\lambda^{2}+\lambda(3k-3h)+ky+hx=0$

$\Rightarrow D>0$

$\Rightarrow 9(k-h)^{2}-8(ky+hx)>0$

$\Rightarrow 9(k-h)^{2}-8(2k^{2}+2h^{2})>0$

$\Rightarrow -7k^{2}-7h^{2}-18kh>0$

$\Rightarrow 7k^{2}+7h^{2}+18kh<0$

$\Rightarrow 7(\frac{1-a}{4})^{2}+7(\frac{1+a}{4})^{2}+18(\frac{1-a^{2}}{16})<0$

$\Rightarrow 7[\frac{2(1+a^{2})}{16}]+\frac{18(1-a^{2})}{16}<0,a^{2}=t$

$\Rightarrow \frac{7}{8}(1+t)+\frac{18(1-t)}{16}<0$

$\Rightarrow \frac{14+14t+18-18t}{16}<0$

$\Rightarrow 4t>32$

$\Rightarrow$ $t>8$

$\Rightarrow$ $a^{2}>8$

questions.question_text: The points of intersection of the line $ax+by=0,(a \ne b)$ and the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-2x=0$ are $A(\alpha,0)$ and $B(1,\beta)$ . The image of the circle with AB as a diameter in the line $x+y+2=0$ is :
questions.question_html: The points of intersection of the line $ax+by=0,(a \ne b)$ and the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-2x=0$ are $A(\alpha,0)$ and $B(1,\beta)$ . The image of the circle with AB as a diameter in the line $x+y+2=0$ is :
questions.explanation_text: As $A$ and $B$ satisfy both line and circle we have $\alpha=0 \Rightarrow A(0,0)$ and $\beta=1$ i.e. $B(1,1)$ Centre of circle as $AB$ diameter is $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})$ and radius $=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\therefore$ For image of $(\frac{1}{2};\frac{1}{2})$ in $x+y+z$ we get $\frac{x-\frac{1}{2}}{1}=\frac{y-\frac{1}{2}}{1}=\frac{-2(3)}{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ Image $(-\frac{5}{2},-\frac{5}{2})$ $\therefore$ Equation of required circle $(x+\frac{5}{2})^{2}+(y+\frac{5}{2})^{2}=\frac{1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}+5x+5y+\frac{50}{4}-\frac{1}{2}=0$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}+5x+5y+12=0$
questions.explanation_html:
As $A$ and $B$ satisfy both line and circle we have $\alpha=0 \Rightarrow A(0,0)$ and $\beta=1$ i.e. $B(1,1)$

Centre of circle as $AB$ diameter is $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})$ and radius $=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

$\therefore$ For image of $(\frac{1}{2};\frac{1}{2})$ in $x+y+z$ we get $\frac{x-\frac{1}{2}}{1}=\frac{y-\frac{1}{2}}{1}=\frac{-2(3)}{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ Image $(-\frac{5}{2},-\frac{5}{2})$

$\therefore$ Equation of required circle

$(x+\frac{5}{2})^{2}+(y+\frac{5}{2})^{2}=\frac{1}{2}$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}+5x+5y+\frac{50}{4}-\frac{1}{2}=0$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}+5x+5y+12=0$

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.question_text: Let the point $(p,p+1)$ lie inside the region $E={(x,y):3-x \le y \le \sqrt{9-x^{2}},0 \le x \le 3}$ . If the set of all values of $p$ is the interval $(a,b)$ , then $b^{2}+b-a^{2}$ is equal to ___________.
questions.question_html: Let the point $(p,p+1)$ lie inside the region $E={(x,y):3-x \le y \le \sqrt{9-x^{2}},0 \le x \le 3}$ . If the set of all values of $p$ is the interval $(a,b)$ , then $b^{2}+b-a^{2}$ is equal to ___________.
questions.explanation_text: Given region, $E={(x,y):3-x \le y \le \sqrt{9-x^{2}},0 \le x \le 3}$ Since, point $(p,p+1)$ lie on line $y=x+1$ $\therefore$ Point of intersection of $y=x+1$ and $y=3-x$ i.e., $x+1=3-x$ $\Rightarrow$ $2x=2 \Rightarrow x=1$ and $y=2$ and point of intersection of $y=x+1$ and $y=\sqrt{9-x^{2}}$ i.e., $(x+1)^{2}=9-x^{2}$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow x^{2}+1+2x=9-x^{2} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 2x^{2}+2x-8=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x^{2}+x-4=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x=\frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{1+4(1)(4)}}{2} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x=\frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow & x=\frac{-1+\sqrt{17}}{2}, & \text{(Since,}x \in [0,3]) \\ \\ \therefore & p \in (1,\frac{-1+\sqrt{17}}{2}) \end{aligned}$ $\Rightarrow a=1,b=\frac{-1+\sqrt{17}}{2}$ $\begin{aligned} & \therefore b^{2}+b-a \\ \\ & =\frac{1+17-2\sqrt{17}}{4}+\frac{(-1+\sqrt{17})}{2}-1 \\ \\ & =\frac{18-2\sqrt{17}-2+2\sqrt{17}-4}{4} \\ \\ & =\frac{12}{4}=3 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given region,

$E={(x,y):3-x \le y \le \sqrt{9-x^{2}},0 \le x \le 3}$

Since, point $(p,p+1)$ lie on line $y=x+1$

$\therefore$ Point of intersection of $y=x+1$ and $y=3-x$

i.e., $x+1=3-x$

$\Rightarrow$ $2x=2 \Rightarrow x=1$

and $y=2$

and point of intersection of $y=x+1$ and

$y=\sqrt{9-x^{2}}$

i.e., $(x+1)^{2}=9-x^{2}$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow x^{2}+1+2x=9-x^{2} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow 2x^{2}+2x-8=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x^{2}+x-4=0 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x=\frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{1+4(1)(4)}}{2} \\ \\ & \Rightarrow x=\frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow & x=\frac{-1+\sqrt{17}}{2}, & \text{(Since,}x \in [0,3]) \\ \\ \therefore & p \in (1,\frac{-1+\sqrt{17}}{2}) \end{aligned}$

$\Rightarrow a=1,b=\frac{-1+\sqrt{17}}{2}$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore b^{2}+b-a \\ \\ & =\frac{1+17-2\sqrt{17}}{4}+\frac{(-1+\sqrt{17})}{2}-1 \\ \\ & =\frac{18-2\sqrt{17}-2+2\sqrt{17}-4}{4} \\ \\ & =\frac{12}{4}=3 \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: Let a triangle ABC be inscribed in the circle $x^{2}-\sqrt{2}(x+y)+y^{2}=0$ such that $\angleBAC=\frac{\pi}{2}$ . If the length of side AB is $\sqrt{2}$ , then the area of the $\Delta$ ABC is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let a triangle ABC be inscribed in the circle $x^{2}-\sqrt{2}(x+y)+y^{2}=0$ such that $\angleBAC=\frac{\pi}{2}$ . If the length of side AB is $\sqrt{2}$ , then the area of the $\Delta$ ABC is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Note: For equation of circle $x^{2}+y^{2}+2gx+2fy+c=0$ , center is $(-g,-f)$ and radius $r=\sqrt{g^{2}+f^{2}-c}$ Given, equation of circle is $x^{2}-\sqrt{2}(x+y)+y^{2}=0$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}-\sqrt{2}x-\sqrt{2}y=0$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}+2(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})x+2(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})=0$ $\therefore$ $g=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $f=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\therefore$ Center $=(-g,-f)=(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})$ And Radius $=r=\sqrt{(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})^{2}+(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})^{2}-0}$ $=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1$ As AB and AC makes an angle 90 $^{\circ}$ then line BC passes through the center of circle and BC is the diameter of the circle. $\therefore$ Length of BC = 2r = 2 $\times$ 1 = 2 $\therefore$ AC 2 = BC 2 $-$ AB 2 = 2 2 $-$ ( $\sqrt{2}$ ) 2 = 2 $\Rightarrow$ AC = $\sqrt{2}$ $\therefore$ Area of right angle triangle ABC = $\frac{1}{2}$ $\times$ AC $\times$ AB = $\frac{1}{2}$ $\times$ $\sqrt{2}$ $\sqrt{2}$ = 1 square unit.
questions.explanation_html:
Note:

For equation of circle $x^{2}+y^{2}+2gx+2fy+c=0$ , center is $(-g,-f)$ and radius $r=\sqrt{g^{2}+f^{2}-c}$

Given,

equation of circle is

$x^{2}-\sqrt{2}(x+y)+y^{2}=0$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}-\sqrt{2}x-\sqrt{2}y=0$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}+2(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})x+2(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})=0$

$\therefore$ $g=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $f=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

$\therefore$ Center $=(-g,-f)=(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})$

And Radius $=r=\sqrt{(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})^{2}+(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})^{2}-0}$

$=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1$

As AB and AC makes an angle 90 $^{\circ}$ then line BC passes through the center of circle and BC is the diameter of the circle.

$\therefore$ Length of BC = 2r = 2 $\times$ 1 = 2

$\therefore$ AC2 = BC2 $-$ AB2

= 22 $-$ ( $\sqrt{2}$ )2

= 2

$\Rightarrow$ AC = $\sqrt{2}$

$\therefore$ Area of right angle triangle ABC

= $\frac{1}{2}$ $\times$ AC $\times$ AB

= $\frac{1}{2}$ $\times$ $\sqrt{2}$ $\sqrt{2}$

= 1 square unit.

questions.question_text: Let the abscissae of the two points P and Q be the roots of $2x^{2}-rx+p=0$ and the ordinates of P and Q be the roots of $x^{2}-sx-q=0$ . If the equation of the circle described on PQ as diameter is $2(x^{2}+y^{2})-11x-14y-22=0$ , then $2r+s-2q+p$ is equal to __________.
questions.question_html: Let the abscissae of the two points P and Q be the roots of $2x^{2}-rx+p=0$ and the ordinates of P and Q be the roots of $x^{2}-sx-q=0$ . If the equation of the circle described on PQ as diameter is $2(x^{2}+y^{2})-11x-14y-22=0$ , then $2r+s-2q+p$ is equal to __________.
questions.explanation_text: Let $P(x_{1},y_{1})$ & $Q(x_{2},y_{2})$ $\therefore$ Roots of $2x^{2}-rx+p=0$ are $x_{1},x_{2}$ and roots of $x^{2}-sx-q=0$ are $y_{1},y_{2}$ . $\therefore$ Equation of circle $\equiv (x-x_{1})(x-x_{2})+(y-y_{1})(y-y_{2})=0$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}-(x_{1}+x_{2})x+x_{1}x_{2}+y^{2}-(y_{1}+y_{2})y+y_{1}y_{2}=0$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}-\frac{r}{2}x+\frac{p}{2}+y^{2}+sy-q=0$ $\Rightarrow 2x^{2}+2y^{2}-rx+2sy+p-2q=0$ Compare with $2x^{2}+2y^{2}-11x-14y-22=0$ We get $r=11,s=7,p-2q=-22$ $\Rightarrow 2r+s+p-2q=22+7-22=7$
questions.explanation_html:
Let $P(x_{1},y_{1})$ & $Q(x_{2},y_{2})$

$\therefore$ Roots of $2x^{2}-rx+p=0$ are $x_{1},x_{2}$

and roots of $x^{2}-sx-q=0$ are $y_{1},y_{2}$ .

$\therefore$ Equation of circle $\equiv (x-x_{1})(x-x_{2})+(y-y_{1})(y-y_{2})=0$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}-(x_{1}+x_{2})x+x_{1}x_{2}+y^{2}-(y_{1}+y_{2})y+y_{1}y_{2}=0$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}-\frac{r}{2}x+\frac{p}{2}+y^{2}+sy-q=0$

$\Rightarrow 2x^{2}+2y^{2}-rx+2sy+p-2q=0$

Compare with $2x^{2}+2y^{2}-11x-14y-22=0$

We get $r=11,s=7,p-2q=-22$

$\Rightarrow 2r+s+p-2q=22+7-22=7$

questions.question_text: Let the tangent to the circle C 1 : x 2 + y 2 = 2 at the point M( $-$ 1, 1) intersect the circle C 2 : (x $-$ 3) 2 + (y $-$ 2) 2 = 5, at two distinct points A and B. If the tangents to C 2 at the points A and B intersect at N, then the area of the triangle ANB is equal to :
questions.question_html: Let the tangent to the circle C1 : x2 + y2 = 2 at the point M( $-$ 1, 1) intersect the circle C2 : (x $-$ 3)2 + (y $-$ 2)2 = 5, at two distinct points A and B. If the tangents to C2 at the points A and B intersect at N, then the area of the triangle ANB is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Equation of tangent at point M is $T=0$ $\Rightarrow xx_{1}+yy_{1}=2$ $\Rightarrow -x+y=2$ $\Rightarrow y=x+2$ Putting this value to equation of circle C 2 , $(x-3)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=5$ $\Rightarrow (x-3)^{2}+x^{2}=5$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}-6x+9+x^{2}=5$ $\Rightarrow 2x^{2}-6x+4=0$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}-3x+2=0$ $\Rightarrow (x-2)(x-1)=0$ $\Rightarrow x=1,2$ when $x=1,$ $y=3$ and when $x=2,$ $y=4$ $\therefore$ Point $A(1,3)$ and $B(2,4)$ Now, equation of tangent at $A(1,3)$ on circle $(x-3)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=5$ or $x^{2}+y^{2}-6x-4y+8=0$ is $T=0$ $xx_{1}+yy_{1}+g(x+x_{1})+f(y+y_{1})+C=0$ $\Rightarrow x+3y-3(x+1)-2(y+3)+8=0$ $\Rightarrow x+3y-3x-3-2y-6+8=0$ $\Rightarrow -2x+y-1=0$ $\Rightarrow 2x-y+1=0$ ....... (1) Similarly tangent at $B(2,4)$ is $2x+4y-3(x+2)-2(y+4)+8=0$ $\Rightarrow 2x+4y-3x-6-2y-8+8=0$ $\Rightarrow -x+2y-6=0$ $\Rightarrow x-2y+6=0$ ...... (2) Solving equation (1) and (2), we get $x-2(2x+1)+6=0$ $\Rightarrow x-4x-2+6=0$ $\Rightarrow -3x+4=0$ $\Rightarrow x=\frac{4}{3}$ $\therefore$ $y=2 \times \frac{4}{3}+1=\frac{11}{3}$ $\therefore$ Point $N=(\frac{4}{3},\frac{11}{3})$ Now area of the triangle ANB $=\frac{1}{2}|\begin{aligned} x_{1} & y_{1} & 1 \\ x_{2} & y_{2} & 1 \\ x_{3} & y_{3} & 1 \end{aligned}|$ $=\frac{1}{2}|\begin{aligned} 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 \\ \frac{4}{3} & \frac{11}{3} & 1 \end{aligned}|$ $=\frac{1}{2}[1(4-\frac{11}{3})-3(2-\frac{4}{3})+1(\frac{22}{3}-\frac{16}{3})]$ $=\frac{1}{2}[\frac{1}{3}-\frac{6}{3}+\frac{6}{3}]$ $=\frac{1}{6}$
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of tangent at point M is

$T=0$

$\Rightarrow xx_{1}+yy_{1}=2$

$\Rightarrow -x+y=2$

$\Rightarrow y=x+2$

Putting this value to equation of circle C2,

$(x-3)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=5$

$\Rightarrow (x-3)^{2}+x^{2}=5$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}-6x+9+x^{2}=5$

$\Rightarrow 2x^{2}-6x+4=0$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}-3x+2=0$

$\Rightarrow (x-2)(x-1)=0$

$\Rightarrow x=1,2$

when $x=1,$ $y=3$

and when $x=2,$ $y=4$

$\therefore$ Point $A(1,3)$ and $B(2,4)$

Now, equation of tangent at $A(1,3)$ on circle $(x-3)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=5$ or $x^{2}+y^{2}-6x-4y+8=0$ is

$T=0$

$xx_{1}+yy_{1}+g(x+x_{1})+f(y+y_{1})+C=0$

$\Rightarrow x+3y-3(x+1)-2(y+3)+8=0$

$\Rightarrow x+3y-3x-3-2y-6+8=0$

$\Rightarrow -2x+y-1=0$

$\Rightarrow 2x-y+1=0$ ....... (1)

Similarly tangent at $B(2,4)$ is

$2x+4y-3(x+2)-2(y+4)+8=0$

$\Rightarrow 2x+4y-3x-6-2y-8+8=0$

$\Rightarrow -x+2y-6=0$

$\Rightarrow x-2y+6=0$ ...... (2)

Solving equation (1) and (2), we get

$x-2(2x+1)+6=0$

$\Rightarrow x-4x-2+6=0$

$\Rightarrow -3x+4=0$

$\Rightarrow x=\frac{4}{3}$

$\therefore$ $y=2 \times \frac{4}{3}+1=\frac{11}{3}$

$\therefore$ Point $N=(\frac{4}{3},\frac{11}{3})$

Now area of the triangle ANB

$=\frac{1}{2}|\begin{aligned} x_{1} & y_{1} & 1 \\ x_{2} & y_{2} & 1 \\ x_{3} & y_{3} & 1 \end{aligned}|$

$=\frac{1}{2}|\begin{aligned} 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 \\ \frac{4}{3} & \frac{11}{3} & 1 \end{aligned}|$

$=\frac{1}{2}[1(4-\frac{11}{3})-3(2-\frac{4}{3})+1(\frac{22}{3}-\frac{16}{3})]$

$=\frac{1}{2}[\frac{1}{3}-\frac{6}{3}+\frac{6}{3}]$

$=\frac{1}{6}$

questions.question_text: $\text{Let}S={(x,y) \in ℕ \times ℕ:9(x-3)^{2}+16(y-4)^{2} \le 144}$ and $T={(x,y) \in ℝ \times ℝ:(x-7)^{2}+(y-4)^{2} \le 36}$ . Then $n(S∩T)$ is equal to __________.
questions.question_html: $\text{Let}S={(x,y) \in ℕ \times ℕ:9(x-3)^{2}+16(y-4)^{2} \le 144}$ and $T={(x,y) \in ℝ \times ℝ:(x-7)^{2}+(y-4)^{2} \le 36}$ . Then $n(S∩T)$ is equal to __________.
questions.explanation_text: $S={(x,y) \in ℕ \times ℕ:\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{16}+\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{9} \le 1}$ represents all the integral points inside and on the ellipse $\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{16}+\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{9}=1$ , in first quadrant. and $T={(x,y) \in ℝ \times ℝ:(x-7)^{2}+(y-4)^{2} \le 36}$ represents all the points on and inside the circle $(x-7)^{2}+(y-4)^{2}=36$ $\therefore n(S∩T)={(3,1),(2,2),(3,2),(4,2),(5,2)$ , $(2,3),\dots(6,5)}$ Total number of points $=27$
questions.explanation_html:
$S={(x,y) \in ℕ \times ℕ:\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{16}+\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{9} \le 1}$

represents all the integral points inside

and on the ellipse $\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{16}+\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{9}=1$ , in first quadrant.

and $T={(x,y) \in ℝ \times ℝ:(x-7)^{2}+(y-4)^{2} \le 36}$ represents all the points on

and inside the circle $(x-7)^{2}+(y-4)^{2}=36$


$\therefore n(S∩T)={(3,1),(2,2),(3,2),(4,2),(5,2)$ , $(2,3),\dots(6,5)}$

Total number of points $=27$

questions.question_text: Let the lines $y+2x=\sqrt{11}+7\sqrt{7}$ and $2y+x=2\sqrt{11}+6\sqrt{7}$ be normal to a circle $C:(x-ℎ)^{2}+(y-k)^{2}=r^{2}$ . If the line $\sqrt{11}y-3x=\frac{5\sqrt{77}}{3}+11$ is tangent to the circle C, then the value of $(5ℎ-8k)^{2}+5r^{2}$ is equal to __________.
questions.question_html: Let the lines $y+2x=\sqrt{11}+7\sqrt{7}$ and $2y+x=2\sqrt{11}+6\sqrt{7}$ be normal to a circle $C:(x-ℎ)^{2}+(y-k)^{2}=r^{2}$ . If the line $\sqrt{11}y-3x=\frac{5\sqrt{77}}{3}+11$ is tangent to the circle C, then the value of $(5ℎ-8k)^{2}+5r^{2}$ is equal to __________.
questions.explanation_text: $L_{1}:y+2x=\sqrt{11}+7\sqrt{7}$ $L_{2}:2y+x=2\sqrt{11}+6\sqrt{7}$ Point of intersection of these two lines is centre of circle i.e. $(\frac{8}{3}\sqrt{7},\sqrt{11}+\frac{5}{3}\sqrt{7})$ $\perp^{r}$ from centre to line $3x-\sqrt{11}y+(\frac{5\sqrt{77}}{3}+11)=0$ is radius of circle $\Rightarrow r=|\frac{8\sqrt{7}-11-\frac{5}{3}\sqrt{77}+\frac{5\sqrt{77}}{3}+11}{\sqrt{20}}|$ $=|\sqrt[4]{}|=\sqrt[4]{}$ units So $(5ℎ-8K)^{2}+5r^{2}$ $=(\frac{40}{3}\sqrt{7}-8\sqrt{11}-\frac{40}{3}\sqrt{7})^{2}+5.16.\frac{7}{5}$ $=64 \times 11+112=816$ .
questions.explanation_html:
$L_{1}:y+2x=\sqrt{11}+7\sqrt{7}$

$L_{2}:2y+x=2\sqrt{11}+6\sqrt{7}$

Point of intersection of these two lines is centre of circle i.e. $(\frac{8}{3}\sqrt{7},\sqrt{11}+\frac{5}{3}\sqrt{7})$

$\perp^{r}$ from centre to line $3x-\sqrt{11}y+(\frac{5\sqrt{77}}{3}+11)=0$ is radius of circle

$\Rightarrow r=|\frac{8\sqrt{7}-11-\frac{5}{3}\sqrt{77}+\frac{5\sqrt{77}}{3}+11}{\sqrt{20}}|$

$=|\sqrt[4]{}|=\sqrt[4]{}$ units

So $(5ℎ-8K)^{2}+5r^{2}$

$=(\frac{40}{3}\sqrt{7}-8\sqrt{11}-\frac{40}{3}\sqrt{7})^{2}+5.16.\frac{7}{5}$

$=64 \times 11+112=816$ .

questions.question_text: For $t \in (0,2\pi)$ , if $ABC$ is an equilateral triangle with vertices $A(sint,-cost),B(cost,sint)$ and $C(a,b)$ such that its orthocentre lies on a circle with centre $(1,\frac{1}{3})$ , then $(a^{2}-b^{2})$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: For $t \in (0,2\pi)$ , if $ABC$ is an equilateral triangle with vertices $A(sint,-cost),B(cost,sint)$ and $C(a,b)$ such that its orthocentre lies on a circle with centre $(1,\frac{1}{3})$ , then $(a^{2}-b^{2})$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Let $P(ℎ,k)$ be the orthocentre of $\Delta$ ABC Then $ℎ=\frac{sint+cost+a}{3},k=\frac{-cost+sint+b}{3}$ (Orthocentre coincide with centroid) $\therefore$ $(3ℎ-a)^{2}+(3k-b)^{2}=2$ $\therefore$ $(ℎ-\frac{a}{3})^{2}+(k-\frac{b}{3})^{2}=\frac{2}{9}$ $\because$ Orthocentre lies on circle with centre $(1,\frac{1}{3})$ $\therefore$ $a=3,b=1$ $\therefore$ $a^{2}-b^{2}=8$
questions.explanation_html:
Let $P(ℎ,k)$ be the orthocentre of $\Delta$ ABC

Then

$ℎ=\frac{sint+cost+a}{3},k=\frac{-cost+sint+b}{3}$

(Orthocentre coincide with centroid)

$\therefore$ $(3ℎ-a)^{2}+(3k-b)^{2}=2$

$\therefore$ $(ℎ-\frac{a}{3})^{2}+(k-\frac{b}{3})^{2}=\frac{2}{9}$

$\because$ Orthocentre lies on circle with centre $(1,\frac{1}{3})$

$\therefore$ $a=3,b=1$

$\therefore$ $a^{2}-b^{2}=8$

questions.question_text: Let the abscissae of the two points $P$ and $Q$ on a circle be the roots of $x^{2}-4x-6=0$ and the ordinates of $P$ and $Q$ be the roots of $y^{2}+2y-7=0$ . If $PQ$ is a diameter of the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}+2ax+2by+c=0$ , then the value of $(a+b-c)$ is _____________.
questions.question_html: Let the abscissae of the two points $P$ and $Q$ on a circle be the roots of $x^{2}-4x-6=0$ and the ordinates of $P$ and $Q$ be the roots of $y^{2}+2y-7=0$ . If $PQ$ is a diameter of the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}+2ax+2by+c=0$ , then the value of $(a+b-c)$ is _____________.
questions.explanation_text: Abscissae of PQ are roots of $x^{2}-4x-6=0$ Ordinates of PQ are roots of $y^{2}+2y-7=0$ and PQ is diameter $\Rightarrow$ Equation of circle is $x^{2}+y^{2}-4x+2y-13=0$ But, given $x^{2}+y^{2}+2ax+2by+c=0$ By comparison $a=-2,b=1,c=-13$ $\Rightarrow a+b-c=-2+1+13=12$
questions.explanation_html:
Abscissae of PQ are roots of $x^{2}-4x-6=0$

Ordinates of PQ are roots of $y^{2}+2y-7=0$

and PQ is diameter

$\Rightarrow$ Equation of circle is

$x^{2}+y^{2}-4x+2y-13=0$

But, given $x^{2}+y^{2}+2ax+2by+c=0$

By comparison $a=-2,b=1,c=-13$

$\Rightarrow a+b-c=-2+1+13=12$
