questions.question_text: If the tangents drawn at the points $O(0,0)$ and $P(1+\sqrt{5},2)$ on the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-2x-4y=0$ intersect at the point Q, then the area of the triangle OPQ is equal to :
questions.question_html: If the tangents drawn at the points $O(0,0)$ and $P(1+\sqrt{5},2)$ on the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-2x-4y=0$ intersect at the point Q, then the area of the triangle OPQ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $tan2\theta=2 \Rightarrow \frac{2tan\theta}{1-tan^{2}\theta}=2$ $tan\theta=\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$ (as $\theta$ is acute) Area $=\frac{1}{2}L^{2}sin2\theta=\frac{1}{2}.\frac{5}{tan^{2}\theta}.2sin\theta cos\theta$ $=\frac{5sin\theta cos\theta}{sin^{2}\theta}.cos^{2}\theta$ $=5cot\theta.cos^{2}\theta$ $=5.\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}-1}.\frac{1}{1+(\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2})^{2}}$ $=\frac{10}{\sqrt{5}-1}.\frac{4}{4+6-2\sqrt{5}}$ $=\frac{40}{2\sqrt{5}(\sqrt{5}-1)^{2}}=\frac{4\sqrt{5}}{6-2\sqrt{5}}$ $=\frac{4\sqrt{5}(6+2\sqrt{5})}{16}$ $=\frac{\sqrt{5}(3+\sqrt{5})}{2}$
questions.explanation_html:
$tan2\theta=2 \Rightarrow \frac{2tan\theta}{1-tan^{2}\theta}=2$

$tan\theta=\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}$ (as $\theta$ is acute)

Area $=\frac{1}{2}L^{2}sin2\theta=\frac{1}{2}.\frac{5}{tan^{2}\theta}.2sin\theta cos\theta$

$=\frac{5sin\theta cos\theta}{sin^{2}\theta}.cos^{2}\theta$

$=5cot\theta.cos^{2}\theta$

$=5.\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}-1}.\frac{1}{1+(\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2})^{2}}$

$=\frac{10}{\sqrt{5}-1}.\frac{4}{4+6-2\sqrt{5}}$

$=\frac{40}{2\sqrt{5}(\sqrt{5}-1)^{2}}=\frac{4\sqrt{5}}{6-2\sqrt{5}}$

$=\frac{4\sqrt{5}(6+2\sqrt{5})}{16}$

$=\frac{\sqrt{5}(3+\sqrt{5})}{2}$

questions.question_text: Let a circle C touch the lines $L_{1}:4x-3y+K_{1}=0$ and $L_{2}=4x-3y+K_{2}=0$ , $K_{1},K_{2} \in R$ . If a line passing through the centre of the circle C intersects L 1 at $(-1,2)$ and L 2 at $(3,-6)$ , then the equation of the circle C is :
questions.question_html: Let a circle C touch the lines $L_{1}:4x-3y+K_{1}=0$ and $L_{2}=4x-3y+K_{2}=0$ , $K_{1},K_{2} \in R$ . If a line passing through the centre of the circle C intersects L1 at $(-1,2)$ and L2 at $(3,-6)$ , then the equation of the circle C is :
questions.explanation_text: Co-ordinate of centre $C \equiv (\frac{3+(-1)}{2},\frac{-6-2}{2}) \equiv (1,-2)$ L 1 is passing through A $\Rightarrow -4-6+K_{1}=0$ $\Rightarrow K_{1}=10$ L 2 is passing through B $\Rightarrow 12+18+K_{2}=0$ $\Rightarrow K_{2}=-30$ Equation of $L_{1}:4x-3y+10=0$ Equation of $L_{2}=4x-3y-30=0$ Diameter of circle $=|\frac{10+30}{\sqrt{4^{2}+(-3)^{2}}}|=8$ $\Rightarrow$ Radius = 4 Equation of circle $(x-1)^{2}+(y+2)^{2}=16$
questions.explanation_html:
Co-ordinate of centre $C \equiv (\frac{3+(-1)}{2},\frac{-6-2}{2}) \equiv (1,-2)$

L1 is passing through A

$\Rightarrow -4-6+K_{1}=0$

$\Rightarrow K_{1}=10$

L2 is passing through B

$\Rightarrow 12+18+K_{2}=0$

$\Rightarrow K_{2}=-30$

Equation of $L_{1}:4x-3y+10=0$

Equation of $L_{2}=4x-3y-30=0$

Diameter of circle $=|\frac{10+30}{\sqrt{4^{2}+(-3)^{2}}}|=8$

$\Rightarrow$ Radius = 4

Equation of circle $(x-1)^{2}+(y+2)^{2}=16$

questions.question_text: Let the mirror image of a circle $c_{1}:x^{2}+y^{2}-2x-6y+\alpha=0$ in line $y=x+1$ be $c_{2}:5x^{2}+5y^{2}+10gx+10fy+38=0$ . If $r$ is the radius of circle $c_{2}$ , then $\alpha+6r^{2}$ is equal to ________.
questions.question_html: Let the mirror image of a circle $c_{1}:x^{2}+y^{2}-2x-6y+\alpha=0$ in line $y=x+1$ be $c_{2}:5x^{2}+5y^{2}+10gx+10fy+38=0$ . If $r$ is the radius of circle $c_{2}$ , then $\alpha+6r^{2}$ is equal to ________.
questions.explanation_text: $c_{1}:x^{2}+y^{2}-2x-6y+\alpha=0$ Then centre $=(1,3)$ and radius $(r)=\sqrt{10-\alpha}$ Image of $(1,3)$ w.r.t. line $x-y+1=0$ is $(2,2)$ $c_{2}:5x^{2}+5y^{2}+10gx+10fy+38=0$ or $x^{2}+y^{2}+2gx+2fy+\frac{38}{5}=0$ Then $(-g,-f)=(2,2)$ $\therefore$ $g=f=-2$ .......... (i) Radius of $c_{2}=r=\sqrt{4+4-\frac{38}{5}}=\sqrt{10-\alpha}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{2}{5}=10-\alpha$ $\therefore$ $\alpha=\frac{48}{5}$ and $r=\sqrt{\frac{2}{5}}$ $\therefore$ $\alpha+6r^{2}=\frac{48}{5}+\frac{12}{5}=12$
questions.explanation_html:
$c_{1}:x^{2}+y^{2}-2x-6y+\alpha=0$

Then centre $=(1,3)$ and radius $(r)=\sqrt{10-\alpha}$

Image of $(1,3)$ w.r.t. line $x-y+1=0$ is $(2,2)$

$c_{2}:5x^{2}+5y^{2}+10gx+10fy+38=0$

or $x^{2}+y^{2}+2gx+2fy+\frac{38}{5}=0$

Then $(-g,-f)=(2,2)$

$\therefore$ $g=f=-2$ .......... (i)

Radius of $c_{2}=r=\sqrt{4+4-\frac{38}{5}}=\sqrt{10-\alpha}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{2}{5}=10-\alpha$

$\therefore$ $\alpha=\frac{48}{5}$ and $r=\sqrt{\frac{2}{5}}$

$\therefore$ $\alpha+6r^{2}=\frac{48}{5}+\frac{12}{5}=12$

Since circle C touches the line L2 at Q intersection point Q of L1 and L2, is (1, $-$ 2)

Now, $PQ=5 \Rightarrow (x-1)^{2}+(\frac{4x+2}{3}-2)^{2}=25$

P(4, $-$ 6)

questions.question_text: Consider three circles: $C_{1}:x^{2}+y^{2}=r^{2}$ $C_{2}:(x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=r^{2}$ $C_{3}:(x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=r^{2}$ If a line L : y = mx + c be a common tangent to C 1 , C 2 and C 3 such that C 1 and C 3 lie on one side of line L while C 2 lies on other side, then the value of $20(r^{2}+c)$ is equal to :
questions.question_html:
Consider three circles:

$C_{1}:x^{2}+y^{2}=r^{2}$

$C_{2}:(x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=r^{2}$

$C_{3}:(x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=r^{2}$

If a line L : y = mx + c be a common tangent to C1, C2 and C3 such that C1 and C3 lie on one side of line L while C2 lies on other side, then the value of $20(r^{2}+c)$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $c_{1}:x^{2}+y^{2}=r^{2}$ ; center = (0, 0) and radius = r $c_{2}:(x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=r^{2}$ ; center = (1, 1) and radius = r $c_{3}:(x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=r^{2}$ ; center = (2, 1) and radius = r Distance of $y=mx+c$ line from center (0, 0) is, $|\frac{0+0+c}{\sqrt{m^{2}+1}}|=r$ ..... (1) Distance of $y=mx+c$ line from center (1, 1) is, $|\frac{m-1+c}{\sqrt{m^{2}+1}}|=r$ ..... (2) Distance of $y=mx+c$ line from center (2, 1) is, $|\frac{2m-1+c}{\sqrt{m^{2}+1}}|=r$ .... (3) From (1) and (2), we get $|\frac{c}{\sqrt{1+m^{2}}}|=|\frac{m-1+c}{\sqrt{1+m^{2}}}|$ $\Rightarrow m-1+c= \pm c$ ..... (4) taking positive sign, $m-1+c=c$ $\Rightarrow m-1=0$ $\Rightarrow m=1$ From (2) and (3), we get $|\frac{m-1+c}{\sqrt{1+m^{2}}}|=|\frac{2m-1+c}{\sqrt{m^{2}+1}}|$ $\Rightarrow (m-1+c)= \pm (2m-1+c)$ ...... (5) taking positive sign, $m-1+c=2m-1+c$ $\Rightarrow m=0$ By taking positive sign we get two different value of m so it is not acceptable. From equation (4), taking negative sign, $m-1+c=-c$ $\Rightarrow m+2c-1=0$ ..... (6) From equation (5), taking negative sign $m-1+c=-(2m-1+c)$ $\Rightarrow 3m+2c-2=0$ ..... (7) Solving equation (6) and (7), we get $3m+1-m-2=0$ $\Rightarrow 2m=1$ $\Rightarrow m=\frac{1}{2}$ $\therefore$ $2c=1-\frac{1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow c=\frac{1}{4}$ Putting value of $m=\frac{1}{2}$ and $c=\frac{1}{4}$ in equation (1), we get $r=|\frac{\frac{1}{4}}{\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4}}}|$ $=|\frac{1}{4} \times \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}|$ $=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}$ $\therefore$ $20(r^{2}+c)$ $=20(\frac{1}{4 \times 5}+\frac{1}{4})$ $=20(\frac{1+5}{20})$ $=6$
questions.explanation_html:
$c_{1}:x^{2}+y^{2}=r^{2}$ ; center = (0, 0) and radius = r

$c_{2}:(x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=r^{2}$ ; center = (1, 1) and radius = r

$c_{3}:(x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=r^{2}$ ; center = (2, 1) and radius = r

Distance of $y=mx+c$ line from center (0, 0) is,

$|\frac{0+0+c}{\sqrt{m^{2}+1}}|=r$ ..... (1)

Distance of $y=mx+c$ line from center (1, 1) is,

$|\frac{m-1+c}{\sqrt{m^{2}+1}}|=r$ ..... (2)

Distance of $y=mx+c$ line from center (2, 1) is,

$|\frac{2m-1+c}{\sqrt{m^{2}+1}}|=r$ .... (3)

From (1) and (2), we get

$|\frac{c}{\sqrt{1+m^{2}}}|=|\frac{m-1+c}{\sqrt{1+m^{2}}}|$

$\Rightarrow m-1+c= \pm c$ ..... (4)

taking positive sign,

$m-1+c=c$

$\Rightarrow m-1=0$

$\Rightarrow m=1$

From (2) and (3), we get

$|\frac{m-1+c}{\sqrt{1+m^{2}}}|=|\frac{2m-1+c}{\sqrt{m^{2}+1}}|$

$\Rightarrow (m-1+c)= \pm (2m-1+c)$ ...... (5)

taking positive sign,

$m-1+c=2m-1+c$

$\Rightarrow m=0$

By taking positive sign we get two different value of m so it is not acceptable.

From equation (4), taking negative sign,

$m-1+c=-c$

$\Rightarrow m+2c-1=0$ ..... (6)

From equation (5), taking negative sign

$m-1+c=-(2m-1+c)$

$\Rightarrow 3m+2c-2=0$ ..... (7)

Solving equation (6) and (7), we get

$3m+1-m-2=0$

$\Rightarrow 2m=1$

$\Rightarrow m=\frac{1}{2}$

$\therefore$ $2c=1-\frac{1}{2}$

$\Rightarrow c=\frac{1}{4}$

Putting value of $m=\frac{1}{2}$ and $c=\frac{1}{4}$ in equation (1), we get

$r=|\frac{\frac{1}{4}}{\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4}}}|$

$=|\frac{1}{4} \times \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}|$

$=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}$

$\therefore$ $20(r^{2}+c)$

$=20(\frac{1}{4 \times 5}+\frac{1}{4})$

$=20(\frac{1+5}{20})$

$=6$

questions.question_html: If the circles $x^{2}+y^{2}+6x+8y+16=0$ and $x^{2}+y^{2}+2(3-\sqrt{3})x+2(4-\sqrt{6})y=k+6\sqrt{3}+8\sqrt{6}$ , $k>0$ , touch internally at the point $P(\alpha,\beta)$ , then $(\alpha+\sqrt{3})^{2}+(\beta+\sqrt{6})^{2}$ is equal to ________________.
questions.explanation_text: The circle $x^{2}+y^{2}+6x+8y+16=0$ has centre $(-3,-4)$ and radius 3 units. The circle $x^{2}+y^{2}+2(3-\sqrt{3})x+2(4-\sqrt{6})y=k+6\sqrt{3}+8\sqrt{6},k>0$ has centre $(\sqrt{3}-3,\sqrt{6}-4)$ and radius $\sqrt{k+34}$ $\because$ These two circles touch internally hence $\sqrt{3+6}=|\sqrt{k+34}-3|$ Here, $k=2$ is only possible ( $\because$ $k>0$ ) Equation of common tangent to two circles is $2\sqrt{3}x+2\sqrt{6}y+16+6\sqrt{3}+8\sqrt{6}+k=0$ $\because$ $k=2$ then equation is $x+\sqrt{2}y+3+4\sqrt{2}+3\sqrt{3}=0$ ...... (i) $\because$ ( $\alpha$ , $\beta$ ) are foot of perpendicular from $(-3,-4)$ To line (i) then $\frac{\alpha+3}{1}=\frac{\beta+4}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{-(-3-4\sqrt{2}+3+4\sqrt{2}+3\sqrt{3})}{1+2}$ $\therefore$ $\alpha+3=\frac{\beta+4}{\sqrt{2}}=-\sqrt{3}$ $\Rightarrow (\alpha+\sqrt{3})^{2}=9$ and $(\beta+\sqrt{6})^{2}=16$ $\therefore$ $(\alpha+\sqrt{3})^{2}+(\beta+\sqrt{6})^{2}=25$
questions.explanation_html:
The circle $x^{2}+y^{2}+6x+8y+16=0$ has centre $(-3,-4)$ and radius 3 units.

The circle $x^{2}+y^{2}+2(3-\sqrt{3})x+2(4-\sqrt{6})y=k+6\sqrt{3}+8\sqrt{6},k>0$ has centre $(\sqrt{3}-3,\sqrt{6}-4)$ and radius $\sqrt{k+34}$

$\because$ These two circles touch internally hence

$\sqrt{3+6}=|\sqrt{k+34}-3|$

Here, $k=2$ is only possible ( $\because$ $k>0$ )

Equation of common tangent to two circles is $2\sqrt{3}x+2\sqrt{6}y+16+6\sqrt{3}+8\sqrt{6}+k=0$

$\because$ $k=2$ then equation is

$x+\sqrt{2}y+3+4\sqrt{2}+3\sqrt{3}=0$ ...... (i)

$\because$ ( $\alpha$ , $\beta$ ) are foot of perpendicular from $(-3,-4)$

To line (i) then

$\frac{\alpha+3}{1}=\frac{\beta+4}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{-(-3-4\sqrt{2}+3+4\sqrt{2}+3\sqrt{3})}{1+2}$

$\therefore$ $\alpha+3=\frac{\beta+4}{\sqrt{2}}=-\sqrt{3}$

$\Rightarrow (\alpha+\sqrt{3})^{2}=9$ and $(\beta+\sqrt{6})^{2}=16$

$\therefore$ $(\alpha+\sqrt{3})^{2}+(\beta+\sqrt{6})^{2}=25$

questions.question_text: Two tangents are drawn from a point P to the circle x 2 + y 2 $-$ 2x $-$ 4y + 4 = 0, such that the angle between these tangents is $tan^{-1}(\frac{12}{5})$ , where $tan^{-1}(\frac{12}{5})$ $\in$ (0, $\pi$ ). If the centre of the circle is denoted by C and these tangents touch the circle at points A and B, then the ratio of the areas of $\Delta$ PAB and $\Delta$ CAB is :
questions.question_html: Two tangents are drawn from a point P to the circle x2 + y2 $-$ 2x $-$ 4y + 4 = 0, such that the angle between these tangents is $tan^{-1}(\frac{12}{5})$ , where $tan^{-1}(\frac{12}{5})$ $\in$ (0, $\pi$ ). If the centre of the circle is denoted by C and these tangents touch the circle at points A and B, then the ratio of the areas of $\Delta$ PAB and $\Delta$ CAB is :
questions.explanation_text: Let $\theta$ = tan $-$ 1 $(\frac{12}{5})$ $\Rightarrow$ tan $\theta$ = $\frac{12}{5}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{2tan\frac{\theta}{2}}{1-tan^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}}=\frac{12}{5}$ $\Rightarrow tan\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{2}{3}$ $\Rightarrow sin\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ and $cos\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}$ In $\Delta$ CAP, $tan\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{1}{AP}$ $\Rightarrow AP=\frac{3}{2}$ In $\Delta$ APM, $sin\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{AM}{AP},cos\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{PM}{AP}$ $\Rightarrow AM=\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}$ $\Rightarrow PM=\frac{9}{2\sqrt{13}}$ $\therefore$ $AB=\frac{6}{\sqrt{13}}$ $\therefore$ Area of $\Delta PAB=\frac{1}{2} \times AB \times PM$ $=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{6}{\sqrt{13}} \times \frac{9}{2\sqrt{13}}=\frac{27}{16}$ Now, $\phi=90^{\circ}-\frac{\theta}{2}$ In $\Delta$ CAM, $cos\phi=\frac{CM}{CA}$ $\Rightarrow CM=1.cos(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\theta}{2})$ $=1.sin\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}$ $\therefore$ Area of $\Delta CAB=\frac{1}{2} \times AB \times CM$ $=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{6}{\sqrt{13}} \times \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}=\frac{6}{13}$ $\therefore$ $\frac{Areaof\Delta PAB}{Areaof\Delta CAB}=\frac{27/26}{6/13}=\frac{9}{4}$ Therefore, the correct answer is (2).
questions.explanation_html:
Let $\theta$ = tan $-$ 1 $(\frac{12}{5})$

$\Rightarrow$ tan $\theta$ = $\frac{12}{5}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{2tan\frac{\theta}{2}}{1-tan^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}}=\frac{12}{5}$

$\Rightarrow tan\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{2}{3}$

$\Rightarrow sin\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ and $cos\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}$

In $\Delta$ CAP,

$tan\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{1}{AP}$

$\Rightarrow AP=\frac{3}{2}$

In $\Delta$ APM,

$sin\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{AM}{AP},cos\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{PM}{AP}$

$\Rightarrow AM=\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}$

$\Rightarrow PM=\frac{9}{2\sqrt{13}}$

$\therefore$ $AB=\frac{6}{\sqrt{13}}$

$\therefore$ Area of $\Delta PAB=\frac{1}{2} \times AB \times PM$

$=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{6}{\sqrt{13}} \times \frac{9}{2\sqrt{13}}=\frac{27}{16}$

Now, $\phi=90^{\circ}-\frac{\theta}{2}$

In $\Delta$ CAM,

$cos\phi=\frac{CM}{CA}$

$\Rightarrow CM=1.cos(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\theta}{2})$

$=1.sin\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}$

$\therefore$ Area of $\Delta CAB=\frac{1}{2} \times AB \times CM$

$=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{6}{\sqrt{13}} \times \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}=\frac{6}{13}$

$\therefore$ $\frac{Areaof\Delta PAB}{Areaof\Delta CAB}=\frac{27/26}{6/13}=\frac{9}{4}$

Therefore, the correct answer is (2).

questions.explanation_text: Radius = $\sqrt{1+4-1}=2$ $AB=\sqrt{3^{2}+2^{2}}=\sqrt{13}$ In $\Delta$ ABP $AP^{2}=AB^{2}-BP^{2}=13-4=9$ AP = 3 AQ = AP = 3 Let $\angle$ ABP = $\theta$ , $\angle$ BAP = 90 $-$ $\theta$ In $\Delta$ ABP, tan $\theta$ = 3/2 $sin\theta=\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}$ , $cos\theta=\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}$ In $\Delta$ ARP, $cos(90-\theta)=\frac{AR}{AP} \Rightarrow AR=3sin\theta$ In $\Delta$ BRP, $cos\theta=\frac{BR}{BP}$ $\Rightarrow BR=2cos\theta=\frac{Area(\Delta APQ)}{Area(\Delta BPQ)}=\frac{\frac{1}{2} \times PQ \times AR}{\frac{1}{2} \times PQ \times BR}$ $=\frac{AR}{RB}=\frac{3sin\theta}{2cos\theta}=\frac{9}{4}$ $\Rightarrow 8(\frac{Area(\Delta APQ)}{Area(\Delta BPQ)})=18$
questions.explanation_html:
Radius = $\sqrt{1+4-1}=2$

$AB=\sqrt{3^{2}+2^{2}}=\sqrt{13}$

In $\Delta$ ABP

$AP^{2}=AB^{2}-BP^{2}=13-4=9$

AP = 3

AQ = AP = 3

Let $\angle$ ABP = $\theta$ , $\angle$ BAP = 90 $-$ $\theta$

In $\Delta$ ABP, tan $\theta$ = 3/2

$sin\theta=\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}$ , $cos\theta=\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}$

In $\Delta$ ARP,

$cos(90-\theta)=\frac{AR}{AP} \Rightarrow AR=3sin\theta$

In $\Delta$ BRP,

$cos\theta=\frac{BR}{BP}$

$\Rightarrow BR=2cos\theta=\frac{Area(\Delta APQ)}{Area(\Delta BPQ)}=\frac{\frac{1}{2} \times PQ \times AR}{\frac{1}{2} \times PQ \times BR}$

$=\frac{AR}{RB}=\frac{3sin\theta}{2cos\theta}=\frac{9}{4}$

$\Rightarrow 8(\frac{Area(\Delta APQ)}{Area(\Delta BPQ)})=18$

questions.question_html: Let the tangent to the circle x2 + y2 = 25 at the point R(3, 4) meet x-axis and y-axis at points P and Q, respectively. If r is the radius of the circle passing through the origin O and having centre at the incentre of the triangle OPQ, then r2 is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Given equation of circle x 2 + y 2 = 25 $\therefore$ Tangent equation at (3, 4) T : 3x + 4y = 25 Incentre of $\Delta$ OPQ. $I=(\frac{\frac{25}{4} \times \frac{25}{3}}{\frac{25}{3}+\frac{25}{4}+\frac{125}{12}},\frac{\frac{25}{3} \times \frac{25}{4}}{\frac{25}{3}+\frac{25}{4}+\frac{125}{12}})$ $\therefore$ $I=(\frac{625}{75+100+125},\frac{625}{75+100+125})=(\frac{25}{12},\frac{25}{12})$ $\because$ Distance from origin to incenter is r. $\therefore$ $r^{2}=(\frac{25}{12})^{2}+(\frac{25}{12})^{2}=\frac{625}{72}$ Therefore, the correct answer is (B).
questions.explanation_html:
Given equation of circle

x2 + y2 = 25

$\therefore$ Tangent equation at (3, 4)

T : 3x + 4y = 25



Incentre of $\Delta$ OPQ.

$I=(\frac{\frac{25}{4} \times \frac{25}{3}}{\frac{25}{3}+\frac{25}{4}+\frac{125}{12}},\frac{\frac{25}{3} \times \frac{25}{4}}{\frac{25}{3}+\frac{25}{4}+\frac{125}{12}})$

$\therefore$ $I=(\frac{625}{75+100+125},\frac{625}{75+100+125})=(\frac{25}{12},\frac{25}{12})$

$\because$ Distance from origin to incenter is r.

$\therefore$ $r^{2}=(\frac{25}{12})^{2}+(\frac{25}{12})^{2}=\frac{625}{72}$

Therefore, the correct answer is (B).

Then the shortest distance from origin to a tangent to this circle which is perpendicular to the line x + 2y = 0, is equal to :
questions.question_html:
Let the lengths of intercepts on x-axis and y-axis made by the circle
x2 + y2 + ax + 2ay + c = 0, (a < 0) be 2 $\sqrt{2}$ and 2 $\sqrt{5}$ , respectively. Then the shortest distance from origin to a tangent to this circle which is perpendicular to the line x + 2y = 0, is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: $2\sqrt{\frac{a^{2}}{4}-c}=2\sqrt{2}$ $\sqrt{a^{2}-4c}=2\sqrt{2}$ $a^{2}-4c=8$ .... (1) $2\sqrt{a^{2}-c}=2\sqrt{5}$ $a^{2}-c=5$ .... (2) $(2)-(1)$ $3c=-3a \Rightarrow c=-1$ $a^{2}=4 \Rightarrow a=-2$ (Given a < 0) Equation of circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-2x-4y-1=0$ Equation of tangent which is perpendicular to the line x + 2y = 0 is $2x-y+\lambda=0$ $\therefore$ p = r $|\frac{2-2+\lambda}{\sqrt{5}}|=\sqrt{6}$ $\Rightarrow \lambda= \pm \sqrt{30}$ $\therefore$ Tangent $2x-y \pm \sqrt{30}=0$ Distance from origin = $\frac{\sqrt{30}}{\sqrt{5}}=\sqrt{6}$
questions.explanation_html:
$2\sqrt{\frac{a^{2}}{4}-c}=2\sqrt{2}$

$\sqrt{a^{2}-4c}=2\sqrt{2}$

$a^{2}-4c=8$ .... (1)

$2\sqrt{a^{2}-c}=2\sqrt{5}$

$a^{2}-c=5$ .... (2)

$(2)-(1)$

$3c=-3a \Rightarrow c=-1$

$a^{2}=4 \Rightarrow a=-2$ (Given a < 0)

Equation of circle

$x^{2}+y^{2}-2x-4y-1=0$

Equation of tangent which is perpendicular to the line x + 2y = 0 is

$2x-y+\lambda=0$

$\therefore$ p = r

$|\frac{2-2+\lambda}{\sqrt{5}}|=\sqrt{6}$

$\Rightarrow \lambda= \pm \sqrt{30}$

$\therefore$ Tangent $2x-y \pm \sqrt{30}=0$

Distance from origin = $\frac{\sqrt{30}}{\sqrt{5}}=\sqrt{6}$

questions.question_html: The diameter of the circle, whose centre lies on the line x + y = 2 in the first quadrant and which touches both the lines x = 3 and y = 2, is _______ .
questions.explanation_text: $\because$ center lies on x + y = 2 and in 1 st quadrant center = ( $\alpha$ , 2 $-$ $\alpha$ ) where $\alpha$ > 0 and 2 $-$ $\alpha$ > 0 $\Rightarrow$ 0 < $\alpha$ < 2 $\because$ circle touches x = 3 and y = 2 $\therefore$ $\frac{|\alpha-3|}{1}=r$ and $\frac{|2-(2-\alpha)|}{1}=r$ $\Rightarrow |\alpha|=r$ $\therefore$ $|\alpha-3|=|\alpha|$ $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha^{2}-6\alpha+9=\alpha^{2}$ $\Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{3}{2}$ $\therefore$ $r=\frac{3}{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ 2r = 3 = diameter.
questions.explanation_html:
$\because$ center lies on x + y = 2 and in 1st quadrant center = ( $\alpha$ , 2 $-$ $\alpha$ )

where $\alpha$ > 0 and 2 $-$ $\alpha$ > 0 $\Rightarrow$ 0 < $\alpha$ < 2

$\because$ circle touches x = 3 and y = 2

$\therefore$ $\frac{|\alpha-3|}{1}=r$

and $\frac{|2-(2-\alpha)|}{1}=r$

$\Rightarrow |\alpha|=r$

$\therefore$ $|\alpha-3|=|\alpha|$

$\Rightarrow$ $\alpha^{2}-6\alpha+9=\alpha^{2}$

$\Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{3}{2}$

$\therefore$ $r=\frac{3}{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ 2r = 3 = diameter.

the line, 3x + 4y = k intersects the circle, x 2 + y 2 – 2x – 4y + 4 = 0 at two distinct points is
______.
questions.question_html:
The number of integral values of k for which the line, 3x + 4y = k intersects the circle,
x2 + y2 – 2x – 4y + 4 = 0 at two distinct points is ______.
questions.explanation_text: Circle x 2 + y 2 – 2x – 4y + 4 = 0 $\Rightarrow$ (x – 1) 2 + (y – 2) 2 = 1 Centre: (1, 2), radius = 1 Line 3x + 4y – k = 0 intersects the circle at two distinct points. $\Rightarrow$ distance of centre from the line < radius $\Rightarrow$ $|\frac{3 \times 1+4 \times 2-k}{\sqrt{3^{2}+4^{2}}}|<1$ $\Rightarrow$ |11 - k| < 5 $\Rightarrow$ 6 < k < 5 $\Rightarrow$ k $\in$ {7, 8, 9, ……15} since k $\in$ I $\therefore$ Total 9 integral value of k.
questions.explanation_html:
Circle x2 + y2 – 2x – 4y + 4 = 0

$\Rightarrow$ (x – 1)2 + (y – 2)2 = 1

Centre: (1, 2), radius = 1

Line 3x + 4y – k = 0 intersects the circle at two distinct points.

$\Rightarrow$ distance of centre from the line < radius

$\Rightarrow$ $|\frac{3 \times 1+4 \times 2-k}{\sqrt{3^{2}+4^{2}}}|<1$

$\Rightarrow$ |11 - k| < 5

$\Rightarrow$ 6 < k < 5

$\Rightarrow$ k $\in$ {7, 8, 9, ……15} since k $\in$ I

$\therefore$ Total 9 integral value of k.

at a point, then the largest value of k is ______.
questions.question_html:
If the curves, x2 – 6x + y2 + 8 = 0 and
x2 – 8y + y2 + 16 – k = 0, (k > 0) touch each other at a point, then the largest value of k is ______.
questions.explanation_text: C 1 : x 2 + y 2 – 6x + + 8 = 0 C 1 (3, 0) and r 1 = 1 C 2 : x 2 + y 2 – 8y + 16 – k = 0 C 2 (0, 4) and r 2 = $\sqrt{k}$ Two circles touch each other $\therefore$ C 1 C 2 = | r 1 $\pm$ r 2 | $\Rightarrow$ 5 = | 1 $\pm$ $\sqrt{k}$ | $\therefore$ 1 + $\sqrt{k}$ = 5 or $\sqrt{k}$ - 1 = 5 $\Rightarrow$ k = 16 or k = 36 So largest value of k = 36.
questions.explanation_html:
C1 : x2 + y2 – 6x + + 8 = 0

C1(3, 0) and r1 = 1

C2 : x2 + y2 – 8y + 16 – k = 0

C2(0, 4) and r2 = $\sqrt{k}$

Two circles touch each other

$\therefore$ C1C2 = | r1 $\pm$ r2 |

$\Rightarrow$ 5 = | 1 $\pm$ $\sqrt{k}$ |

$\therefore$ 1 + $\sqrt{k}$ = 5 or $\sqrt{k}$ - 1 = 5

$\Rightarrow$ k = 16 or k = 36

So largest value of k = 36.

$\therefore$ Length of chord of contact (AB) = $\frac{8}{\sqrt{5}}$

questions.explanation_text: S 1 $\equiv$ x 2 + y 2 + 5Kx + 2y + K = 0 $S_{2} \equiv x^{2}+y^{2}+Kx+\frac{3}{2}y-\frac{1}{2}=0$ Equation of common chord is S 1 – S 2 = 0 $\Rightarrow 4Kx+\frac{y}{2}+K+\frac{1}{2}=0$ ....(1) 4x + 5y – K = 0 …(2) (given) On comparing (1) and (2) $\frac{4K}{4}=\frac{1}{10}=\frac{2K+1}{-2K}$ $\Rightarrow K=\frac{1}{10}$ and $-2K=20K+10$ $\Rightarrow$ 22K = –10 $\therefore K=\frac{-5}{11}$ So No value of K exists.

Equation of common chord is

S1 – S2 = 0

$\Rightarrow 4Kx+\frac{y}{2}+K+\frac{1}{2}=0$ ....(1)

4x + 5y – K = 0 …(2) (given)

On comparing (1) and (2)

$\frac{4K}{4}=\frac{1}{10}=\frac{2K+1}{-2K}$

$\Rightarrow K=\frac{1}{10}$ and $-2K=20K+10$

$\Rightarrow$ 22K = –10

$\therefore K=\frac{-5}{11}$

So No value of K exists.

questions.explanation_text: x 2 + y 2 + 4x $-$ 6y $-$ 12 = 0 Equation of tangent at (1, $-$ 1) x $-$ y + 2(x + 1) $-$ 3(y $-$ 1) $-$ 12 = 0 3x $-$ 4y $-$ 7 = 0 $\therefore$ Equation of circle is (x 2 + y 2 + 4x $-$ 6y $-$ 12) + $\lambda$ (3x $-$ 4y $-$ 7) = 0 It passes through (4, 0) : (16 + 16 $-$ 12) + $\lambda$ (12 $-$ 7) = 0 $\Rightarrow$ 20 + $\lambda$ (5) = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda$ = $-$ 4 $\therefore$ (x 2 + y 2 + 4x $-$ 6y $-$ 12) $-$ 4(3x $-$ 4y $-$ 7) = 0 or   x 2 + y 2 $-$ 8x + 10y + 16 = 0 Radius = $\sqrt{16+25-16}=5$

$\therefore$    Equation of circle is

Radius = $\sqrt{16+25-16}=5$

questions.explanation_text: Let the point of tangency A(cos $\theta$ , sin $\theta$ ) Equation of tangent at A, xcos $\theta$ + ysin $\theta$ = 1 $\therefore$ P(sec $\theta$ , 0) and Q(0, cosec $\theta$ ) Let M(h, k) is the mid-point of PQ. $\therefore$ h = $\frac{sec\theta+0}{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ 2h = sec $\theta$ $\Rightarrow$ cos $\theta$ = $\frac{1}{2ℎ}$ .....(1) $\therefore$ k = $\frac{cosec\theta+0}{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ 2k = cosec $\theta$ $\Rightarrow$ sin $\theta$ = $\frac{1}{2k}$ .....(2) From (1) and (2), sin 2 $\theta$ + cos 2 $\theta$ = $(\frac{1}{2ℎ})^{2}+(\frac{1}{2k})^{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{4ℎ^{2}}+\frac{1}{4k^{2}}=1$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{ℎ^{2}+k^{2}}{4ℎ^{2}k^{2}}=1$ $\Rightarrow$ $ℎ^{2}+k^{2}=4ℎ^{2}k^{2}$ $\therefore$ Locus of the midpoint, x 2 + y 2 – 4x 2 y 2 = 0

$\therefore$ P(sec $\theta$ , 0) and Q(0, cosec $\theta$ )

Let M(h, k) is the mid-point of PQ.

$\therefore$ h = $\frac{sec\theta+0}{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ 2h = sec $\theta$

$\Rightarrow$ cos $\theta$ = $\frac{1}{2ℎ}$ .....(1)

$\therefore$ k = $\frac{cosec\theta+0}{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ 2k = cosec $\theta$

$\Rightarrow$ sin $\theta$ = $\frac{1}{2k}$ .....(2)

From (1) and (2),

sin2 $\theta$ + cos2 $\theta$ = $(\frac{1}{2ℎ})^{2}+(\frac{1}{2k})^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{4ℎ^{2}}+\frac{1}{4k^{2}}=1$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{ℎ^{2}+k^{2}}{4ℎ^{2}k^{2}}=1$

$\Rightarrow$ $ℎ^{2}+k^{2}=4ℎ^{2}k^{2}$

$\therefore$ Locus of the midpoint,

x2 + y2 – 4x2y2 = 0

questions.question_text: If the tangent at (1, 7) to the curve x 2 = y - 6 touches the circle x 2 + y 2 + 16x + 12y + c = 0, then the value of c is :
questions.question_html:
If the tangent at (1, 7) to the curve x2 = y - 6

touches the circle x2 + y2 + 16x + 12y + c = 0, then the value of c is :
questions.explanation_text: NOTE : Equation of tangent at (x 1 , y 1 ) to the curve x 2 = 4ay is xx 1 = 4a $(\frac{y+y_{1}}{2})$ Now equation of tangent at (1, 7) to x 2 = y $-$ 6 is $x.1=4.\frac{1}{4}(\frac{y+7}{2})-6$ $\Rightarrow 2x=y+7-12$ $\Rightarrow 2x-y+5=0$ This tangent touches the circle. So, perpendicular distance from the center of the circle to the tangent is equal to the radius of the circle. For the circle, $x^{2}+y^{2}+16x+12y+C=0$ center is ( $-$ 8, $-$ 6) and radius (r) = $\sqrt{8^{2}+6^{2}-c}$ $=\sqrt{100-c}$ Distance of the tangent from the center of the circle d = $|\frac{2(-8)-(-6)+5}{\sqrt{2^{2}+1^{2}}}|$ $=|\frac{-16+6+5}{\sqrt{5}}|$ And we know d = r $\therefore$ $|\frac{-16+11}{\sqrt{5}}|=\sqrt{100-c}$ $\Rightarrow |\frac{-5}{\sqrt{5}}|=\sqrt{100-c}$ $\Rightarrow |-\sqrt{5}|=\sqrt{100-c}$ $\Rightarrow 5=100-c$ $\Rightarrow c=95$
questions.explanation_html:
NOTE :

Equation of tangent at (x1, y1) to the curve x2 = 4ay is

xx1 = 4a $(\frac{y+y_{1}}{2})$

Now equation of tangent at (1, 7) to x2 = y $-$ 6 is

$x.1=4.\frac{1}{4}(\frac{y+7}{2})-6$

$\Rightarrow 2x=y+7-12$

$\Rightarrow 2x-y+5=0$

This tangent touches the circle.



So, perpendicular distance from the center of the circle to the tangent is equal to the radius of the circle.

For the circle,

$x^{2}+y^{2}+16x+12y+C=0$

center is ( $-$ 8, $-$ 6)

and radius (r) = $\sqrt{8^{2}+6^{2}-c}$

$=\sqrt{100-c}$

Distance of the tangent from the center of the circle

d = $|\frac{2(-8)-(-6)+5}{\sqrt{2^{2}+1^{2}}}|$

$=|\frac{-16+6+5}{\sqrt{5}}|$

And we know d = r

$\therefore$ $|\frac{-16+11}{\sqrt{5}}|=\sqrt{100-c}$

$\Rightarrow |\frac{-5}{\sqrt{5}}|=\sqrt{100-c}$

$\Rightarrow |-\sqrt{5}|=\sqrt{100-c}$

$\Rightarrow 5=100-c$

$\Rightarrow c=95$

questions.question_text: A circle passes through the points (2, 3) and (4, 5). If its centre lies on the line, $y-4x+3=0,$ then its radius is equal to :
questions.question_html: A circle passes through the points (2, 3) and (4, 5). If its centre lies on the line, $y-4x+3=0,$ then its radius is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Centre $(\alpha,\beta)$ lies on line $y-4x+3=0$ Then, $\beta=4\alpha-3$ And $\text{Radius}=\sqrt{(\alpha-2)^{2}+(\beta-3)^{2}}=\sqrt{(\alpha-4)^{2}+(\beta-5)^{2}}$ $\begin{aligned} & \alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+13-4\alpha-6\beta=\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+41-8\alpha-10\beta \\ \\ & 4\alpha+4\beta=28 \Rightarrow \alpha+\beta=7 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha+4\alpha-3=7 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=2,\beta=5 \end{aligned}$ Therefore, Radius $=\sqrt{(2-2)^{2}+(5-3)^{2}}=2$
questions.explanation_html:
Centre $(\alpha,\beta)$ lies on line $y-4x+3=0$

Then, $\beta=4\alpha-3$

And

$\text{Radius}=\sqrt{(\alpha-2)^{2}+(\beta-3)^{2}}=\sqrt{(\alpha-4)^{2}+(\beta-5)^{2}}$

$\begin{aligned} & \alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+13-4\alpha-6\beta=\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+41-8\alpha-10\beta \\ \\ & 4\alpha+4\beta=28 \Rightarrow \alpha+\beta=7 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha+4\alpha-3=7 \\ \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=2,\beta=5 \end{aligned}$

Therefore, Radius $=\sqrt{(2-2)^{2}+(5-3)^{2}}=2$

questions.question_text:
The two adjacent sides of a cyclic quadrilateral are 2 and 5 and the angle between them is 60 o . If the area of the quadrilateral is $4\sqrt{3}$ , then the perimeter
of the quadrilateral is :
questions.question_html: The two adjacent sides of a cyclic quadrilateral are 2 and 5 and the angle between them is 60o. If the area of the quadrilateral is $4\sqrt{3}$ , then the perimeter of the quadrilateral is :
questions.explanation_text: Here; cos $\theta$ = $\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}-c^{2}}{2ab}$ and $\theta$ = 60 o $\Rightarrow$ cos 60 o = $\frac{4+25-c^{2}}{2.2.5}$ $\Rightarrow$ 10 = 29 $-$ c 2 $\Rightarrow$ c 2 = 19 $\Rightarrow$ c = $\sqrt{19}$ also;  cos $\theta$ = $\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}-c^{2}}{2ab}$ and $\theta$ = 120 o $\Rightarrow$ $-$ $\frac{1}{2}$ = $\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}-19}{2ab}$ $\Rightarrow$ a 2 + b 2 $-$ 19 = $-$ ab $\Rightarrow$ a 2 + b 2 + ab = 19 $\therefore$ Area = $\frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 5$ sin 60 + $\frac{1}{2}$ ab sin 120 o = 4 $\sqrt{3}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2}+\frac{ab\sqrt{3}}{4}$ = $4\sqrt{3}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{ab}{4}$ = 4 $-$ $\frac{5}{2}$ = $\frac{3}{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ ab = 6 $\therefore$ a 2 + b 2 = 13 $\Rightarrow$ a = 2, b = 3 Perimeter = Sum of all sides = 2 + 5 + 2 + 3 = 12
questions.explanation_html:
Here; cos $\theta$  =  $\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}-c^{2}}{2ab}$

and   $\theta$ = 60o

$\Rightarrow$    cos 60o = $\frac{4+25-c^{2}}{2.2.5}$

$\Rightarrow$     10 = 29 $-$ c2

$\Rightarrow$    c2 = 19

$\Rightarrow$    c = $\sqrt{19}$

also;  cos $\theta$ = $\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}-c^{2}}{2ab}$

and $\theta$ = 120o

$\Rightarrow$     $-$ $\frac{1}{2}$ = $\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}-19}{2ab}$

$\Rightarrow$    a2 + b2 $-$ 19 = $-$ ab

$\Rightarrow$    a2 + b2 + ab = 19

$\therefore$    Area = $\frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 5$ sin 60 + $\frac{1}{2}$ ab sin 120o = 4 $\sqrt{3}$

$\Rightarrow$     $\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2}+\frac{ab\sqrt{3}}{4}$ = $4\sqrt{3}$

$\Rightarrow$     $\frac{ab}{4}$ = 4 $-$ $\frac{5}{2}$ = $\frac{3}{2}$

$\Rightarrow$     ab = 6

$\therefore$    a2 + b2 = 13

$\Rightarrow$    a = 2, b = 3

Perimeter = Sum of all sides

= 2 + 5 + 2 + 3 = 12

questions.question_html: If a point P has co-ordinates (0, $-$ 2) and Q is any point on the circle, x2 + y2 $-$ 5x $-$ y + 5 = 0, then the maximum value of (PQ)2 is :
questions.explanation_text: Given that x 2 + y 2 $-$ 5x $-$ y + 5 = 0 $\Rightarrow$ (x $-$ 5/2) 2 $-$ $\frac{25}{4}$ + (y $-$ 1/2) 2 $-$ 1/4 = 0 $\Rightarrow$ (x $-$ 5/2) 2 + (y $-$ 1/2) 2 = 3/2 on circle [ Q $\equiv$ (5/2 + $\sqrt{3/2}$ cos Q, $\frac{1}{2}$ + $\sqrt{3/2}$ sin Q)] $\Rightarrow$ PQ 2 = $(\frac{5}{2}+\sqrt{3/2}cosQ)^{2}$ + $(\frac{5}{2}+\sqrt{3/2}sinQ)^{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ PQ 2 = $\frac{25}{2}+\frac{3}{2}+5\sqrt{3/2}$ (cos Q + sinQ) = 14 + 5 $\sqrt{3/2}$ (cosQ + sinQ) $\therefore$ Maximum value of PQ 2 = 14 + 5 $\sqrt{3/2}$ $\times$ $\sqrt{2}$ = 14 + 5 $\sqrt{3}$

$\Rightarrow$    (x $-$ 5/2)2 $-$ $\frac{25}{4}$ + (y $-$ 1/2)2 $-$ 1/4 = 0

$\Rightarrow$    (x $-$ 5/2)2 + (y $-$ 1/2)2 = 3/2

on circle [ Q $\equiv$ (5/2 + $\sqrt{3/2}$ cos Q, $\frac{1}{2}$ + $\sqrt{3/2}$ sin Q)]

$\Rightarrow$    PQ2 = $\frac{25}{2}+\frac{3}{2}+5\sqrt{3/2}$ (cos Q + sinQ)

= 14 + 5 $\sqrt{3/2}$ (cosQ + sinQ)

$\therefore$    Maximum value of PQ2

= 14 + 5 $\sqrt{3/2}$ $\times$   $\sqrt{2}$ = 14 + 5 $\sqrt{3}$

questions.question_html: If two parallel chords of a circle, having diameter 4units, lie on the opposite sides of the center and subtend angles $cos^{-1}(\frac{1}{7})$ and sec $-$ 1 (7) at the center respectivey, then the distance between these chords, is :
questions.explanation_text: Since cos2 $\theta$ = 1/7 $\Rightarrow$ 2 cos 2 Q $-$ 1 = 1/7 $\Rightarrow$ 2 cos 2 $\theta$ = 8/7 $\Rightarrow$ cos 2 $\theta$ = 4/7 $\Rightarrow$ cos 2 $\theta$ = $\frac{4}{7}$ $\Rightarrow$ cos 2 $\theta$ = $\frac{2}{\sqrt{7}}$ Also, sec 2 $\phi$ = 7 = $\frac{1}{2cos^{2}\phi-1}$ 7 = cos 2 $\phi$ $-$ 1 = $\frac{1}{7}$ = 2 cos 2 $\phi$ = $\frac{8}{7}$ = cos $\phi$ = $\frac{2}{\sqrt{7}}$ P 1 P 2 = r cos $\theta$ + r cos $\phi$ = $\frac{4}{\sqrt{7}}+\frac{4}{\sqrt{7}}$ = $\frac{8}{\sqrt{7}}$
questions.explanation_html:
Since cos2 $\theta$ = 1/7   $\Rightarrow$  2 cos2 Q $-$ 1 = 1/7

$\Rightarrow$    2 cos2 $\theta$ = 8/7

$\Rightarrow$     cos2 $\theta$ = 4/7

$\Rightarrow$     cos2 $\theta$ = $\frac{4}{7}$

$\Rightarrow$    cos2 $\theta$ = $\frac{2}{\sqrt{7}}$

Also, sec2 $\phi$ = 7 = $\frac{1}{2cos^{2}\phi-1}$ 7

= cos2 $\phi$ $-$ 1 = $\frac{1}{7}$

= 2 cos2 $\phi$ = $\frac{8}{7}$

= cos $\phi$ = $\frac{2}{\sqrt{7}}$

P1P2 = r cos $\theta$ + r cos $\phi$

= $\frac{4}{\sqrt{7}}+\frac{4}{\sqrt{7}}$ = $\frac{8}{\sqrt{7}}$

questions.explanation_text: Equation of circle $C \equiv (x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=1$ Radius of $T=|y|$ $T$ touches $C$ externally therefore, Distance between the centers $=$ sum of their radii $\Rightarrow \sqrt{(0-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}}=1+|y|$ $\Rightarrow (0-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=(1+|y|)^{2}$ $\Rightarrow 1+y^{2}+1-2y=1+y^{2}+2|y|$ $2|y|=1-2y$ If $y>0$ then $2y=1-2y$ $\Rightarrow y=\frac{1}{4}$ $y<0$ then $-2y=1-2y$ $\Rightarrow 0=1$ (not possible) $\therefore$ $y=\frac{1}{4}$

questions.question_html: Three distinct points A, B and C are given in the 2 -dimensional coordinates plane such that the ratio of the distance of any one of them from the point $(1,0)$ to the distance from the point $(-1,0)$ is equal to $\frac{1}{3}$ . questions.explanation_text: Given that $P(1,0),Q(-1,0)$ and $\frac{AP}{AQ}=\frac{BP}{BQ}=\frac{CP}{CQ}=\frac{1}{3}$ $\Rightarrow 3AP=AQ$ Let $A=(x,y)$ then $3AP=AQ \Rightarrow 9AP^{2}=AQ^{2}$ $\Rightarrow 9(x-1)^{2}+9y^{2}=(x+1)^{2}+y^{2}$ $\Rightarrow 9x^{2}-18x+9+9y^{2}=x^{2}+2x+1+y^{2}$ $\Rightarrow 8x^{2}-20x+8y^{2}+8=0$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}-\frac{5}{3}x+1=0...(1)$ $\therefore$ A lies on the circle given by eq. $(1).$ As $B$ and $C$ also follow the same condition, - they must lie on the same circle. $\therefore$ Center of circumcircle of $\Delta ABC$ $=$ Center of circle given by $(1)=(\frac{5}{4},0)$
questions.explanation_html:

$P(1,0),Q(-1,0)$

and $\frac{AP}{AQ}=\frac{BP}{BQ}=\frac{CP}{CQ}=\frac{1}{3}$

$\therefore$ A lies on the circle given by eq. $(1).$ As $B$ and $C$

also follow the same condition, - they must lie on the same circle.

$\therefore$ Center of circumcircle of $\Delta ABC$

$=$ Center of circle given by $(1)=(\frac{5}{4},0)$

$\Rightarrow (x^{2}+y^{2}+3x+7y+2p-5)+\lambda$

$(x+5y+p^{2}+2p-5)=0$

As it passes through $(1,1),$ therefore

$\Rightarrow (7+2p)+\lambda(2p+p^{2}+1)=0$

$\Rightarrow \lambda=-\frac{2p+7}{(p+1)},$

which does not exist for $p=-1$

questions.question_html: If the pair of lines $ax^{2}+2(a+b)xy+by^{2}=0$ lie along diameters of a circle and divide the circle into four sectors such that the area of one of the sectors is thrice the area of another sector then :
questions.explanation_text: As per question area of one sector $=3$ area of another sector $\Rightarrow$ at center by one sector $=3 \times$ angle at center by another sector Let one angle be $\theta$ then other $=30$ Clearly $\theta+3\theta=180 \Rightarrow \theta=45^{\circ}$ $\therefore$ Angle between the diameters represented by combined equation $ax^{2}+2(a+bxy)+by^{2}=0$ is $45^{\circ}$ $\therefore$ Using $tan$ $\theta$ $=\frac{2\sqrt{ℎ^{2}-ab}}{a+b}$ we get $tan45^{\circ}=\frac{2\sqrt{(a+b)^{2}-ab}}{a+b}$ $\Rightarrow 1=\frac{2\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+ab}}{a+b}$ $\Rightarrow (a+b)^{2}=4(a^{2}+b^{2}+ab)$ $\Rightarrow a^{2}+b^{2}+2ab=4a^{2}+4b^{2}+4ab$ $\Rightarrow 3a^{2}+3b^{2}+2ab=0$
questions.explanation_html:
As per question area of one sector $=3$ area of another sector

$\Rightarrow$ at center by one sector $=3 \times$ angle at center by another sector

Let one angle be $\theta$ then other $=30$

$\therefore$ Angle between the diameters represented by combined equation

$ax^{2}+2(a+bxy)+by^{2}=0$ is $45^{\circ}$

$\therefore$ Using $tan$ $\theta$ $=\frac{2\sqrt{ℎ^{2}-ab}}{a+b}$

we get $tan45^{\circ}=\frac{2\sqrt{(a+b)^{2}-ab}}{a+b}$

$\Rightarrow 1=\frac{2\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+ab}}{a+b}$

$\Rightarrow (a+b)^{2}=4(a^{2}+b^{2}+ab)$

$\Rightarrow a^{2}+b^{2}+2ab=4a^{2}+4b^{2}+4ab$

$\Rightarrow 3a^{2}+3b^{2}+2ab=0$

questions.question_text: If a circle passes through the point (a, b) and cuts the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=p^{2}$ orthogonally, then the equation of the locus of its centre is :
questions.question_html: If a circle passes through the point (a, b) and cuts the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=p^{2}$ orthogonally, then the equation of the locus of its centre is :
questions.explanation_text: Let the center be $(\alpha,\beta)$ As It cuts the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=p^{2}$ orthogonally $\therefore$ Using $2g_{1}g_{2}+2f_{1}f_{2}=c_{1}+c_{2},$ we get $2(-\alpha) \times 0+2(-\beta) \times 0$ $=c_{1}-p^{2} \Rightarrow c_{1}=p^{2}$ Let equation of circle is $x^{2}+y^{2}-2\alpha x-2\beta y+p^{2}=0$ It passes through $(a,b) \Rightarrow a^{2}+b^{2}-2\alpha a-2\beta b+p^{2}=0$ $\therefore$ Locus of $(\alpha,\beta)$ is $\therefore$ $2ax+2by-(a^{2}+b^{2}+p^{2})=0.$
questions.explanation_html:
Let the center be $(\alpha,\beta)$

As It cuts the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=p^{2}$ orthogonally

$\therefore$ Using $2g_{1}g_{2}+2f_{1}f_{2}=c_{1}+c_{2},$ we get

$2(-\alpha) \times 0+2(-\beta) \times 0$

$=c_{1}-p^{2} \Rightarrow c_{1}=p^{2}$

Let equation of circle is

$x^{2}+y^{2}-2\alpha x-2\beta y+p^{2}=0$

It passes through

$(a,b) \Rightarrow a^{2}+b^{2}-2\alpha a-2\beta b+p^{2}=0$

$\therefore$ Locus of $(\alpha,\beta)$ is

$\therefore$ $2ax+2by-(a^{2}+b^{2}+p^{2})=0.$

questions.question_text: A circle touches the x-axis and also touches the circle with centre at (0, 3) and radius 2. The locus of the centre of the circle is :
questions.question_html: A circle touches the x-axis and also touches the circle with centre at (0, 3) and radius 2. The locus of the centre of the circle is :
questions.explanation_text: Equation of circle with center $(0,3)$ and radius $2$ is $x^{2}+(y-3)^{2}=4$ Let locus of the variable circle is $(\alpha,\beta)$ As it touches $x$ -axis. $\therefore$ It's equation is $(x-\alpha)^{2}+(y+\beta)^{2}=\beta^{2}$ Circle touch externally $\Rightarrow c_{1}c_{2}=r_{1}+r_{2}$ $\therefore$ $\sqrt{\alpha^{2}+(\beta-3)^{2}}=2+\beta$ $\alpha^{2}+(\beta-3)^{2}=\beta^{2}+4+4\beta$ $\Rightarrow \alpha^{2}=10(\beta-1/2)$ $\therefore$ Locus is $x^{2}=10(y-\frac{1}{2})$ which is parabola.
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of circle with center $(0,3)$ and radius $2$ is

$x^{2}+(y-3)^{2}=4$

Let locus of the variable circle is $(\alpha,\beta)$

As it touches $x$ -axis.

$\therefore$ It's equation is $(x-\alpha)^{2}+(y+\beta)^{2}=\beta^{2}$



Circle touch externally $\Rightarrow c_{1}c_{2}=r_{1}+r_{2}$

$\therefore$ $\sqrt{\alpha^{2}+(\beta-3)^{2}}=2+\beta$

$\alpha^{2}+(\beta-3)^{2}=\beta^{2}+4+4\beta$

$\Rightarrow \alpha^{2}=10(\beta-1/2)$

$\therefore$ Locus is $x^{2}=10(y-\frac{1}{2})$ which is parabola.

questions.question_text: If the lines 2x + 3y + 1 + 0 and 3x - y - 4 = 0 lie along diameter of a circle of circumference $10\pi$ , then the equation of the circle is :
questions.question_html: If the lines 2x + 3y + 1 + 0 and 3x - y - 4 = 0 lie along diameter of a circle of circumference $10\pi$ , then the equation of the circle is :
questions.explanation_text: Two diameters are along $2x+3y+1=0$ and $3x-y-4=0$ solving we get center $(1,-1)$ circumference $=2\pi r=10\pi$ $\therefore$ $r=5$ . Required circle is, $(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}=5^{2}$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}-2x+2y-23=0$
questions.explanation_html:
Two diameters are along

$2x+3y+1=0$ and $3x-y-4=0$

solving we get center $(1,-1)$

circumference $=2\pi r=10\pi$

$\therefore$ $r=5$ .

Required circle is, $(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}=5^{2}$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}-2x+2y-23=0$

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.question_text: If a circle passes through the point (a, b) and cuts the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=4$ orthogonally, then the locus of its centre is :
questions.question_html: If a circle passes through the point (a, b) and cuts the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=4$ orthogonally, then the locus of its centre is :
questions.explanation_text: Let the variable circle is $x^{2}+y^{2}+2gx+2fy+c=0...(1)$ It passes through $(a,b)$ $\therefore$ $a^{2}+b^{2}+2ga+2fb+c=0...(2)$ $(1)$ cuts $x^{2}+y^{2}=4$ orthogonally $\therefore$ $2(g \times 0+f \times 0)=c-4 \Rightarrow c=4$ $\therefore$ from $(2)$ $a^{2}+b^{2}+2ga+2fb+4=0$ $\therefore$ Locus of center $(-g,-f)$ is $a^{2}+b^{2}-2ax-2by+4=0$ or $2ax+2by=a^{2}+b^{2}+4$
questions.explanation_html:
Let the variable circle is

$x^{2}+y^{2}+2gx+2fy+c=0...(1)$

It passes through $(a,b)$

$\therefore$ $a^{2}+b^{2}+2ga+2fb+c=0...(2)$

$(1)$ cuts $x^{2}+y^{2}=4$ orthogonally

$\therefore$ $2(g \times 0+f \times 0)=c-4 \Rightarrow c=4$

$\therefore$ from $(2)$ $a^{2}+b^{2}+2ga+2fb+4=0$

$\therefore$ Locus of center $(-g,-f)$ is

$a^{2}+b^{2}-2ax-2by+4=0$

or $2ax+2by=a^{2}+b^{2}+4$

questions.question_text: Intercept on the line y = x by the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-2x=0$ is AB. Equation of the circle on AB as a diameter is :
questions.question_html: Intercept on the line y = x by the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-2x=0$ is AB. Equation of the circle on AB as a diameter is :
questions.explanation_text: Solving $y=x$ and the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-2x=0,$ we get $x=0,y=0$ and $x=1,$ $y=1$ $\therefore$ Extremities of diameter of the required circle are $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ . Hence, the equation of circle is $(x-0)(x-1)+(y-0)(y-1)=0$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}-x-y=0$
questions.explanation_html:
Solving $y=x$ and the circle

$x^{2}+y^{2}-2x=0,$ we get

$x=0,y=0$ and $x=1,$ $y=1$

$\therefore$ Extremities of diameter of the required circle are

$(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ . Hence, the equation of circle is

$(x-0)(x-1)+(y-0)(y-1)=0$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}-x-y=0$

questions.question_text: A variable circle passes through the fixed point A (p, q) and touches x-axis. The locus of the other end of the diameter through A is :
questions.question_html: A variable circle passes through the fixed point A (p, q) and touches x-axis. The locus of the other end of the diameter through A is :
questions.explanation_text: Let the variable circle be $x^{2}+y^{2}+2gx+2fy+c=0...(1)$ $\therefore$ $p^{2}+q^{2}+2gp+2fq+c=0...(2)$ Circle $(1)$ touches $x$ -axis, $\therefore$ $g^{2}-c=0 \Rightarrow c=g^{2}.$ From $(2)$ $p^{2}+q^{2}+2gp+2fq+g^{2}=0...(3)$ Let the other end of diameter through $(p,q)$ be $(ℎ,k),$ then, $\frac{ℎ+p}{2}=-g$ and $\frac{k+q}{2}=-f$ Put in $(3)$ $p^{2}+q^{2}+2p(-\frac{ℎ+p}{2})+2q(-\frac{k+q}{2})+(\frac{ℎ+p}{2})^{2}=0$ $\Rightarrow ℎ^{2}+p^{2}-2ℎp-4kq=0$ $\therefore$ locus of $(ℎ,k)$ is $x^{2}+p^{2}-2xp-4yq=0$ $\Rightarrow (x-p)^{2}=4qy$
questions.explanation_html:
Let the variable circle be

$x^{2}+y^{2}+2gx+2fy+c=0...(1)$

$\therefore$ $p^{2}+q^{2}+2gp+2fq+c=0...(2)$

Circle $(1)$ touches $x$ -axis,

$\therefore$ $g^{2}-c=0 \Rightarrow c=g^{2}.$

From $(2)$

$p^{2}+q^{2}+2gp+2fq+g^{2}=0...(3)$

Let the other end of diameter through $(p,q)$ be $(ℎ,k),$

then, $\frac{ℎ+p}{2}=-g$ and $\frac{k+q}{2}=-f$

Put in $(3)$

$p^{2}+q^{2}+2p(-\frac{ℎ+p}{2})+2q(-\frac{k+q}{2})+(\frac{ℎ+p}{2})^{2}=0$

$\Rightarrow ℎ^{2}+p^{2}-2ℎp-4kq=0$

$\therefore$ locus of $(ℎ,k)$ is $x^{2}+p^{2}-2xp-4yq=0$

$\Rightarrow (x-p)^{2}=4qy$

questions.question_html: The lines 2x - 3y = 5 and 3x - 4y = 7 are diameters of a circle having area as 154 sq. units. Then the equation of the circle is :
questions.explanation_text: $\pi r^{2}=154 \Rightarrow r=7$ For center on solving equation $2x-3y=5&3x-4y=7$ we get $x=1,y=-1$ $\therefore$ center $=(1,-1)$ Equation of circle, $(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}=7^{2}$ $x^{2}+y^{2}-2x+2y=47$
questions.explanation_html:
$\pi r^{2}=154 \Rightarrow r=7$

For center on solving equation

$2x-3y=5&3x-4y=7$

we get $x=1,y=-1$

$\therefore$ center $=(1,-1)$

Equation of circle,

$(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}=7^{2}$

$x^{2}+y^{2}-2x+2y=47$

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.question_text: If the chord y = mx + 1 of the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=1$ subtends an angle of measure $45^{\circ}$ at the major segment of the circle then value of m is :
questions.question_html: If the chord y = mx + 1 of the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=1$ subtends an angle of measure $45^{\circ}$ at the major segment of the circle then value of m is :

options.label: D
options.html: none of these

questions.explanation_text: Equation of circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=1=(1)^{2}$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}=(y-mx)^{2}$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}=m^{2}x^{2}-2mxy;$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}(1-m^{2})+2mxy=0.$ Which represents the pair of lines between which the angle is $45^{\circ}.$ $tan45= \pm \frac{2\sqrt{m^{2}-0}}{1-m^{2}}=\frac{\pm 2m}{1-m^{2}};$ $\Rightarrow 1-m^{2}= \pm 2m$ $\Rightarrow m^{2} \pm 2m-1=0$ $\Rightarrow m=\frac{-2 \pm \sqrt{4+4}}{2}$ $=\frac{-2 \pm 2\sqrt{2}}{2}$ $=-1 \pm \sqrt{2}.$
questions.explanation_html:
Equation of circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=1=(1)^{2}$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}=(y-mx)^{2}$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}=m^{2}x^{2}-2mxy;$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}(1-m^{2})+2mxy=0.$

Which represents the pair of lines between which the angle is $45^{\circ}.$

$tan45= \pm \frac{2\sqrt{m^{2}-0}}{1-m^{2}}=\frac{\pm 2m}{1-m^{2}};$

$\Rightarrow 1-m^{2}= \pm 2m$

$\Rightarrow m^{2} \pm 2m-1=0$

$\Rightarrow m=\frac{-2 \pm \sqrt{4+4}}{2}$

$=\frac{-2 \pm 2\sqrt{2}}{2}$

$=-1 \pm \sqrt{2}.$

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.question_text: The centre of the circle passing through (0, 0) and (1, 0) and touching the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=9$ is :
questions.question_html: The centre of the circle passing through (0, 0) and (1, 0) and touching the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=9$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Let the required circle be $x^{2}+y^{2}+2gx+2fy+c=0$ Since it passes through $(0,0)$ and $(1,0)$ $\Rightarrow c=0$ and $g=-\frac{1}{2}$ Points $(0,0)$ and $(1,0)$ lie inside the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=9,$ so two circles touch internally $\Rightarrow c_{1}c_{2}=r_{1}-r_{2}$ $\therefore$ $\sqrt{g^{2}+f^{2}}=3-\sqrt{g^{2}+f^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow \sqrt{g^{2}+f^{2}}=\frac{3}{2}$ $\Rightarrow f^{2}=\frac{9}{4}-\frac{1}{4}=2$ $\therefore$ $f= \pm \sqrt{2}.$ Hence, the centers of required circle are $(\frac{1}{2}.\sqrt{2})$ or $(\frac{1}{2},-\sqrt{2})$
questions.explanation_html:
Let the required circle be

$x^{2}+y^{2}+2gx+2fy+c=0$

Since it passes through $(0,0)$ and $(1,0)$

$\Rightarrow c=0$ and $g=-\frac{1}{2}$

Points $(0,0)$ and $(1,0)$ lie inside the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=9,$

so two circles touch internally

$\Rightarrow c_{1}c_{2}=r_{1}-r_{2}$

$\therefore$ $\sqrt{g^{2}+f^{2}}=3-\sqrt{g^{2}+f^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow \sqrt{g^{2}+f^{2}}=\frac{3}{2}$

$\Rightarrow f^{2}=\frac{9}{4}-\frac{1}{4}=2$

$\therefore$ $f= \pm \sqrt{2}.$

Hence, the centers of required circle are

$(\frac{1}{2}.\sqrt{2})$ or $(\frac{1}{2},-\sqrt{2})$

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.question_text: The equation of a circle with origin as a center and passing through an equilateral triangle whose median is of length $3$ $a$ is :
questions.question_html: The equation of a circle with origin as a center and passing through an equilateral triangle whose median is of length $3$ $a$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Let $ABC$ be an equilateral triangle, whose median is $AD.$ Given $AD=3a.$ In $\Delta ABD,AB^{2}=AD^{2}+BD^{2};$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}=9a^{2}+(x^{2}/4)$ where $AB=BC=AC=x.$ $\frac{3}{4}x^{2}=9a^{2} \Rightarrow x^{2}=12a^{2}.$ In $\Delta OBD,OB^{2}=OD^{2}+BD^{2}$ $\Rightarrow r^{2}=(3a-r)^{2}+\frac{x^{2}}{4}$ $\Rightarrow r^{2}=9a^{2}-6ar+r^{2}+3a^{2};$ $\Rightarrow 6ar=12a^{2}$ $\Rightarrow r=2a$ So equation of circle is $x^{2}+y^{2}=4a^{2}$
questions.explanation_html:
Let $ABC$ be an equilateral triangle, whose median is $AD.$



Given $AD=3a.$

In $\Delta ABD,AB^{2}=AD^{2}+BD^{2};$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}=9a^{2}+(x^{2}/4)$

where $AB=BC=AC=x.$

$\frac{3}{4}x^{2}=9a^{2} \Rightarrow x^{2}=12a^{2}.$

In $\Delta OBD,OB^{2}=OD^{2}+BD^{2}$

$\Rightarrow r^{2}=(3a-r)^{2}+\frac{x^{2}}{4}$

$\Rightarrow r^{2}=9a^{2}-6ar+r^{2}+3a^{2};$

$\Rightarrow 6ar=12a^{2}$

$\Rightarrow r=2a$

So equation of circle is $x^{2}+y^{2}=4a^{2}$
